facts.text: Cooper's hawk nicknames include big blue darter, flying cross, quail hawk and swift hawk.
facts.quote: Other common names for Cooper's hawk include: big blue darter, chicken hawk, flying cross, hen hawk, quail hawk, striker, and swift hawk.

facts.text: Breeding Cooper's hawks may use well over 40 claimed call variations, though the differences are probably quite subtle.
facts.quote: During breeding, Cooper's hawks may utter well over 40 claimed call variations, which would rank them as having among the most varied collection of such for any raptor, but probably quite subtle (marginal differences in harshness, clarity, tempo and volume).

facts.text: Cooper's hawks sometimes hunt in tandem, one dashing after prey while another waits on the far side of a tree trunk or thicket.
facts.quote: Sometimes, Cooper's hawks engage in tandem hunts with one dashing around after the prey, while another waits on the other side of a tree trunk or wooded thicket.

facts.text: Young Cooper's hawks have rarely been reported lying on their backs on a branch, apparently as a form of sunning.
facts.quote: Although a rare behavior, several cases of juvenile hawks proning, wherein they lie on their backs along a branch (or rarely the ground), apparently as a form of sunning, have been reported.

facts.text: Young Cooper's hawks are impetuous about crashing into bushes after prey, even thorny barberries; adults are said to be more prudent.
facts.quote: Young Cooper's hawks are impetuous about crashing into bushes after prey, sometimes even into thorny cover such as barberries, whereas adults are said to be more "prudent".

facts.text: Female spotted sandpipers may mate with and lay eggs for more than one male, leaving the incubating to the males.
facts.quote: During each summer breeding season, females may mate with and lay clutches for more than one male, leaving incubation to them.

facts.text: Male spotted sandpipers take care of the chicks both before and after they hatch.
facts.quote: Male spotted sandpipers take care of the offspring, both before and after the offspring hatch.

facts.text: Spotted sandpipers can catch insects in flight, and they also eat small fish and carrion.
facts.quote: They may also catch insects in flight. They eat insects (such as flies, beetles, grasshoppers, mayflies, midges, crickets and caterpillars), crustaceans and other invertebrates (such as spiders, snails, other molluscs, and worms), as well as small fish and carrion.

facts.text: Spotted sandpipers have a distinctive walk in which their tails bob up and down.
facts.quote: They also have a distinctive walk in which their tails bob up and down.

facts.text: Stray spotted sandpipers may settle down with common sandpipers and hybridize.
facts.quote: They replace each other geographically; stray birds may settle down with breeders of the other species and hybridize.

facts.text: In one experiment, 64% of males with their red shoulder patches dyed black lost their territories, versus 8% of the control males.
facts.quote: When the red shoulder patches were dyed black as part of an experiment, 64% of males lost their territories, while only 8% of control subjects did.

facts.text: Bird counts of wintering red-winged blackbirds sometimes show loose flocks of more than a million birds.
facts.quote: Claims have been made that it is the most abundant living land bird in North America, as bird-counting censuses of wintering red-winged blackbirds sometimes show that loose flocks can number in excess of a million birds per flock and the full number of breeding pairs across North and Central America may exceed 250 million in peak years.

facts.text: Female red-winged blackbirds sing too, typically a scolding chatter.
facts.quote: The female also sings, typically a scolding chatter chit chit chit chit chit chit cheer teer teer teerr.

facts.text: Wood duck chicks can jump from as high as 50 feet and survive by landing in water or on soft leaf litter.
facts.quote: Chicks can jump from as high as 50 feet, surviving by landing either in water, or on top of soft material such as leaf litter.

facts.text: When nest boxes are too close together, females may lay eggs in their neighbors' nests, a habit called "nest dumping."
facts.quote: However, if nesting boxes are placed too close together, females may lay eggs in the nests of their neighbours, which may lead to nests with thirty eggs or more and unsuccessful incubation—a behaviour known as "nest dumping".

facts.text: In southern regions, a wood duck can produce two broods in a single season, something no other North American duck can do.
facts.quote: Unlike most other ducks, the wood duck has sharp claws for perching in trees and can, in southern regions, produce two broods in a single season—the only North American duck that can do so.

facts.text: Wood ducks can crush acorns in their gizzard after swallowing them.
facts.quote: They are able to crush acorns after swallowing them within their gizzard.

facts.text: Fulda, Minnesota, has adopted the wood duck as an unofficial mascot and has a large number of nest boxes.
facts.quote: Fulda, Minnesota, has adopted the wood duck as an unofficial mascot, and a large number of nest boxes can be found in the area.

facts.text: The grasshopper sparrow is named for its song, a high trill that sounds like a grasshopper and follows a series of short chips.
facts.quote: The primary male song, a high trill preceded by a stereotyped series of short chips, is reminiscent of the sounds of grasshoppers and is the origin of this species' name.

facts.text: Grasshopper sparrows build dome-shaped nests on the ground, with a small side opening, well hidden in the grass.
facts.quote: Grasshopper sparrows build inconspicuous, dome-shaped nests on the ground, typically very well hidden amongst grasses and forbs. The nests have a small side opening and are usually made of a mix of dead and live grasses.

facts.text: Males that migrated north averaged about 2,500 km over about 30 days, traveling roughly 82 km a day.
facts.quote: Individuals migrated an average of ~2,500 km over ~30 days. Birds migrate mostly over land, make few stop-overs of short duration, and travel at about 82 km/day.

facts.text: In Florida, some invasive snakes, including Burmese pythons and green anacondas, may eat grasshopper sparrows.
facts.quote: In Florida, grasshopper sparrows may be eaten by some growth stage of invasive snakes such as Burmese pythons, Reticulated pythons, Southern African rock pythons, Central African rock pythons, boa constrictors, yellow anacondas, Bolivian anacondas, dark-spotted anacondas, and green anacondas.

facts.text: The color teal is named after this little duck.
facts.quote: The bird gives its name to the blue-green colour teal.

facts.text: Its species name imitates the male's call, the 'duck that says cryc.'
facts.quote: The specific name of Linnaeus is thus onomatopoetic, the "duck that says cryc"; the common names in Norwegian krikkand, Danish krikand, and German Krickente mean the same, referring to the male's characteristic call which was already discussed by Linnaeus' sources.

facts.text: Teal ducklings weigh just 15 grams when they hatch.
facts.quote: They are recognisable by their tiny size however, weighing just 15 g (0.53 oz) at hatching.

facts.text: Once the females start laying, the males leave and gather in flocks on lakes to molt.
facts.quote: After the females have started laying, the males leave them and move away for shorter or longer distances, assembling in flocks on particular lakes where they moult into eclipse plumage; they will usually encounter their offspring only in winter quarters.

facts.text: London mallards are much louder than rural Cornwall mallards, a bit like a regional accent for ducks.
facts.quote: Research conducted by Middlesex University on two English mallard populations found that the vocalisations of the mallard varies depending on their environment and have something akin to a regional accent, with urban mallards in London being much louder and more vociferous compared to rural mallards in Cornwall, serving as an adaptation to persistent levels of anthropogenic noise.

facts.text: Sleeping with one eye open, so half the brain stays alert, was first demonstrated in mallards.
facts.quote: The predation-avoidance behaviour of sleeping with one eye open, allowing one brain hemisphere to remain aware while the other half sleeps, was first demonstrated in mallards, although it is believed to be widespread among birds in general.

facts.text: In 2019, a pair of common loons in Wisconsin were seen raising an abandoned mallard duckling for several weeks.
facts.quote: However, in 2019, a pair of common loons in Wisconsin were observed raising a mallard duckling for several weeks, having seemingly adopted the bird after it had been abandoned by its parents.

facts.text: Outside the breeding season, a large flock of mallards is known as a "sordes".
facts.quote: It is highly gregarious outside of the breeding season and forms large flocks, which are known as "sordes".

facts.text: When a mallard takes off, its wings make a faint whistling noise.
facts.quote: When taking off, the wings of a mallard produce a characteristic faint whistling noise.

facts.text: Mated sandhill cranes sing synchronized duets, and the female makes two calls for every one from the male.
facts.quote: The cranes stand close together, calling in a synchronized and complex duet. The female makes two calls for every one from the male.

facts.text: Sandhill cranes can stay aloft for many hours on thermals, needing only occasional wing flaps.
facts.quote: Using thermals to obtain lift, they can stay aloft for many hours, requiring only occasional flapping of their wings, thus expending little energy.

facts.text: Sandhill crane chicks hatch with their eyes open and can leave the nest within a day.
facts.quote: The chicks are precocial; they hatch covered in down, with their eyes open, and able to leave the nest within a day.

facts.text: West Virginia's Mothman is thought to have originated from sightings of sandhill cranes that were out of migration.
facts.quote: The mythical Mothman, a humanoid creature reportedly seen in the Point Pleasant, West Virginia, area from November 1966 to December 1967, is thought to have originated from sightings of out-of-migration sandhill cranes.

facts.text: A sandhill crane can kill a predator, even a coyote, by piercing its skull with its sharp beak.
facts.quote: It can even kill predators by piercing through the skull with its sharp beak, and even coyotes can be killed.

facts.text: A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart can beat up to 1260 times per minute.
facts.quote: Hummingbirds have one of the highest metabolic rates of any animal, with heart rates up to 1260 beats per minute, breathing rate of about 250 breaths per minute even at rest, and oxygen consumption of about 4 ml oxygen/g/hour at rest.

facts.text: Hummingbird nests have even been found on loops of chain, wire, and extension cords.
facts.quote: Nests have even been found on loops of chain, wire, and extension cords.

facts.text: The female builds her nest from bud scales and lichen, bound together with spider's silk.
facts.quote: The nest is composed of bud scales, with lichen on the exterior, bound with spider's silk, and lined with fibers such as plant down (often dandelion or thistle down) and animal hair.

facts.text: During courtship, a male makes a rapid tik-tik sound with his wings as he flies side to side in front of a female.
facts.quote: During the courtship displays, the male makes a rapid tik-tik tik-tik tik-tik sound with his wings.

facts.text: Great egrets aren't usually noisy, but at breeding colonies they often give a loud croaking "cuk cuk cuk."
facts.quote: The great egret is not normally a vocal bird; it gives a low, hoarse croak when disturbed, and at breeding colonies, it often gives a loud croaking cuk cuk cuk and higher-pitched squawks.

facts.text: Great egrets fly with their necks pulled in, unlike storks, cranes, ibises and spoonbills, which stretch their necks out.
facts.quote: Its flight is slow with its neck retracted. This is characteristic of herons and bitterns, and distinguishes them from storks, cranes, ibises, and spoonbills, which extend their necks in flight.

facts.text: Around the end of the 19th century, many North American great egrets were killed for their plumes, called "aigrettes," to decorate hats.
facts.quote: In North America, large numbers of great egrets were killed around the end of the 19th century so that their plumes, known as "aigrettes", could be used to decorate hats.

facts.text: In 2018, a pair of great egrets nested in Finland for the first time, raising four young in a grey heron colony.
facts.quote: In 2018, a pair of great egrets nested in Finland for the first time, raising four young in a grey heron colony in Porvoo.

facts.text: A photo of a great egret in breeding plumage is on the cover of Faith No More's 1992 album Angel Dust.
facts.quote: An airbrushed photograph of a great egret in breeding plumage by Werner Krutein is featured in the cover art of the 1992 Faith No More album Angel Dust.

facts.text: Great blue herons usually swallow their food whole, and they have been known to choke on prey that is too large.
facts.quote: Herons locate their food by sight and usually swallow it whole. They have been known to choke on prey that is too large.

facts.text: In flight, herons bend their necks into an S shape, while cranes hold theirs straight.
facts.quote: Herons and cranes are easiest to differentiate in flight; cranes hold their necks straight when flying, but herons bend theirs into an S shape.

facts.text: A great blue heron's stick nest starts around 50 cm across but can grow to more than 120 cm wide with repeated use.
facts.quote: Nests are usually around 50 cm (20 in) across when first constructed, but can grow to more than 120 cm (47 in) in width and 90 cm (35 in) deep with repeated use and additional construction.

facts.text: Great blue herons can take on sizeable snakes, including water snakes 105 cm long.
facts.quote: They can take on sizeable snakes, including water snakes 105 cm (41 in) in length.

facts.text: Tufted titmice sometimes pluck hair from live mammals to line their nests, a behavior called kleptotrichy.
facts.quote: They line the nest with soft materials, sometimes plucking hair from live mammals to use as material, a behavior known as kleptotrichy.

facts.text: If a tufted titmouse finds shed snakeskin, it may weave pieces of it into its nest.
facts.quote: If they find snakeskin sheddings, they may incorporate pieces into their nest.

facts.text: Young tufted titmice often stay with their parents through winter, and sometimes help raise the next year's chicks.
facts.quote: Unlike many birds, the offspring of tufted titmice  often stay with their parents during the winter and even after the first year of their lives. Sometimes, a bird born the year before helps its parents raise the next year's young.

facts.text: At a feeder, a tufted titmouse takes one seed per visit and stores seeds within 130 feet of the feeder.
facts.quote: When visiting a feeder, they take one seed per visit and store seeds within 130 feet of the feeder.

facts.text: A group of tufted titmice is called a troupe or a banditry.
facts.quote: This species readily forms small flocks, known as troupes or banditries, which often associate with chickadees and other passerines when foraging.

facts.text: When only one bird can reach a twig's berries, a flock may line up and pass them beak-to-beak down the line.
facts.quote: When the end of a twig holds a supply of berries that only one bird at a time can reach, members of a flock may line up along the twig and pass berries beak-to-beak down the line so that each bird gets a chance to eat.

facts.text: During courtship, a pair sits together and passes small objects back and forth, such as flower petals or an insect.
facts.quote: During courtship, the male and female sit together and pass small objects back and forth, such as flower petals or an insect.

facts.text: A female may make up to 2,500 trips while building her nest, which takes around five or six days.
facts.quote: Around five or six days are needed for the female waxwing to build the nest, with up to 2,500 trips back and forth.

facts.text: Sometimes a waxwing eats overripe fruit that has begun to ferment, which intoxicates the bird.
facts.quote: Sometimes, cedar waxwings eat fruit that is overripe and has begun to ferment, intoxicating the bird.

facts.text: A male does a hopping dance for the female, and if she is interested, she hops back.
facts.quote: The male does a "hopping dance" for the female. If she is interested, she will hop back.

facts.text: The oldest recorded Canada goose was a 33-year-old female first tagged in Ohio in 1969.
facts.quote: The oldest recorded individual was a 33-year-old female first tagged in Ohio in 1969.

facts.text: Canada goose goslings can walk, swim, and find their own food as soon as they hatch.
facts.quote: As soon as the goslings hatch, they are immediately capable of walking, swimming, and finding their own food (a diet similar to that of adult geese).

facts.text: The giant Canada goose was believed extinct in the 1950s until a small flock was found wintering in Minnesota in 1962.
facts.quote: The giant Canada goose subspecies was believed to be extinct in the 1950s until, in 1962, a small flock was discovered wintering in Rochester, Minnesota, by Harold Hanson of the Illinois Natural History Survey.

facts.text: Geese flying in a V rotate the front position, because flying in front uses the most energy.
facts.quote: The front position is rotated since flying in front consumes the most energy.

facts.text: In 2009, a flock of migratory Canada geese cost US Airways Flight 1549 power in both engines, forcing it down into the Hudson River.
facts.quote: In 2009, a collision with a flock of migratory Canada geese resulted in US Airways Flight 1549 suffering a total loss of power from both engines after takeoff, forcing the crew of the aircraft to ditch the plane in the Hudson River with no loss of human life.

facts.text: A red-tailed hawk's scream is often used as a generic raptor sound effect on TV, even when the bird on screen isn't a red-tail.
facts.quote: The fierce, screaming cry of the red-tailed hawk is frequently used as a generic raptor sound effect in television shows and other media, even if the bird featured is not a red-tailed hawk.

facts.text: A Central Park hawk nicknamed Pale Male became the star of a nonfiction book called Red-Tails in Love.
facts.quote: One famous urban red-tailed hawk, known as "Pale Male", became the subject of a nonfiction book, Red-Tails in Love: A Wildlife Drama in Central Park, and is the first known red-tail in decades to successfully nest and raise young in the crowded New York City borough of Manhattan.

facts.text: Red-tailed hawks have been seen hunting in pairs, stalking opposite sides of a tree to trap a squirrel between them.
facts.quote: Red-tailed hawks, like some other raptors, have been observed to hunt in pairs. This may consist of stalking opposites sides of a tree, to surround a tree squirrel and almost inevitably drive the rodent to be captured by one after being flushed by the other hawk.

facts.text: Hawks have been seen following American badgers to catch the prey the badgers flush out.
facts.quote: Hawks have been observed following American badgers to capture prey they flush, and the two are considered potential competitors.

facts.text: Great horned owls can't build nests, so they typically take over existing red-tail nests.
facts.quote: Great horned owls are incapable of constructing nests and typically expropriate existing red-tail nests.

facts.text: Blue jays and Steller's jays sometimes imitate the red-shouldered hawk's call, and it's hard to tell them from the hawk by voice alone.
facts.quote: Steller's jays and blue jays, both of which being potential prey species, sometimes habitually imitate the call of the red-shouldered hawk and are known to be difficult to distinguish on voice alone.

facts.text: Red-shouldered hawks often reuse the same nest year after year, adding fresh sticks to it each spring.
facts.quote: They often use the same nest year after year, refurbishing it annually with sticks in the spring.

facts.text: Males sometimes perform a sky-dance: soaring high, then making a series of steep dives, each followed by a wide spiral and rapid ascent.
facts.quote: Males may also perform the "sky-dance" by soaring high in the air, and then making a series of steep dives, each followed by a wide spiral and rapid ascent.

facts.text: In Florida, red-shouldered hawks sometimes team up with American crows to mob shared enemies like great horned owls.
facts.quote: In Florida, red-shouldered hawks sometimes collaborate and peaceably coexist with American crows (usually an enemy to all other birds because of their egg-hunting habits) so they cooperatively mob mutual predators, mainly great horned owls and red-tailed hawks.

facts.text: Red-shouldered hawk chicks hatch at different times, with the first one hatching up to a week before the last.
facts.quote: Hatching is asynchronous, with the first chick hatching up to a week before the last.

facts.text: The broad-winged hawk's call is a very high-pitched kee-ee that sounds almost like a whistle.
facts.quote: Their call sounds like a very high-pitched kee-ee, almost like a whistle.

facts.text: In courtship, broad-winged hawks meet in midair, hook their feet together and spiral down together.
facts.quote: Birds meet in the air, hook their feet together and spiral down together.

facts.text: Fall migration for these hawks lasts 70 days, covering about 100 km (62 mi) a day without crossing salt water.
facts.quote: Fall migration lasts for 70 days as birds migrate about 100 km (62 mi) per day from North America, through Central America to South America without crossing salt water.

facts.text: Green herons use bait to fish, dropping items like bread, feathers or mayflies on the water to lure fish within reach.
facts.quote: Green herons have been observed using captured prey (e.g. mayflies) or other objects (bread, feathers) to "bait-fish", using a lure on the water's surface to attract fish.

facts.text: In cities, green herons have been known to eat goldfish.
facts.quote: Some of the many fish eaten are minnows, sunfish, catfish, perch, eels and, in urban areas, goldfish.

facts.text: A male green heron courts a female by flying in front of her noisily, with his head and neck feathers puffed up.
facts.quote: The pairs form in the breeding range, after an intense courtship display by the males, who select the nesting sites and fly in front of the female noisily and with puffed-up head and neck plumage.

facts.text: Green herons can hover briefly to catch prey.
facts.quote: They are able to hover briefly to catch prey.

facts.text: Green heron eggs are pale green, and the parents take turns keeping them warm for about 19 to 21 days.
facts.quote: The clutch is usually 2–6 pale green eggs, which are laid in two-day intervals (though the second egg may be laid up to six days later than the first). After the last egg has been laid, both parents incubate for about 19–21 days until hatching, and feed the young birds.

facts.text: Cox's sandpiper, once described as its own species, turned out to be a hybrid of the pectoral sandpiper and the curlew sandpiper.
facts.quote: Cox's sandpiper, originally described as a new species Calidris paramelanotos, has proven to be a stereotyped hybrid between this species and the curlew sandpiper.

facts.text: A pectoral sandpiper's eggs sit about 3 cm below ground level in the nest, which helps cut heat loss from cool breezes.
facts.quote: The nest is deep enough that the eggs sit about 3 cm (1.2 in) below ground level, which helps to minimize heat loss from the cool breezes which occur at the latitudes where the species nests.

facts.text: In breeding season, a male pectoral sandpiper puffs up his breast, which has a fat sac, to boost his courtship display.
facts.quote: The male has a courtship display which involves puffing up his breast, which has a fat sac in the breeding season to enhance his performance.

facts.text: In September 2003, a record 40 pectoral sandpipers turned up in Ireland and 150 in Great Britain.
facts.quote: September 2003 saw a record influx to those two countries, with 40 found in Ireland and 150 in Great Britain.

facts.text: Pectoral sandpipers passing through northern Ohio now mostly head north in April, versus early-mid May 100 years ago.
facts.quote: The pectoral sandpiper's migration might be affected by global warming, as is suspected for many Arctic-breeding birds; 100 years ago, migrating pectoral sandpipers were observed to pass through northern Ohio in early-mid May and again in late August; today, the bulk of the northward migration takes place in April, and most birds do not return until mid-September.

facts.text: While migrating through Delaware Bay, least sandpipers eat worms, detritus, and horseshoe crab eggs.
facts.quote: While migrating through the Delaware Bay, least sandpipers eat worms, detritus, and the eggs of horseshoe crabs.

facts.text: The name minutilla is Medieval Latin for "very small".
facts.quote: The specific minutilla is Medieval Latin for "very small".

facts.text: A male cardinal may mistake his reflection for an invading male and fight it relentlessly.
facts.quote: He may mistake his image on various reflective surfaces as an invading male and will fight his reflection relentlessly.

facts.text: During courtship, a male cardinal collects food and feeds it to the female beak-to-beak.
facts.quote: During courtship they may also participate in a bonding behavior where the male collects food and brings it to the female, feeding her beak-to-beak.

facts.text: Cardinals can drop their body temperature by 3 to 6 °F if needed to survive cold temperatures.
facts.quote: Cardinals have the ability to drop their body temperature 3 to 6 °F (1.7 to 3.3 °C) if needed in order to survive cold temperatures.

facts.text: A female cardinal crushes twigs with her beak until they bend easily, then shapes them into a cup around her body with her feet.
facts.quote: She crushes twigs with her beak until they are pliable, then turns in the nest to bend the twigs around her body and push them into a cup shape with her feet.

facts.text: Cardinal songs are learned, so they vary from one region to another.
facts.quote: The northern cardinal learns its songs, and as a result the songs vary regionally.

facts.text: Veeries sing less often and for shorter stretches when they hear a barred owl recording, possibly to avoid becoming prey.
facts.quote: Veeries have been shown to decrease the rate and duration of singing when exposed to barred owl playback, possibly to decrease the chance of predation.

facts.text: Veeries flip over leaves on the forest floor to uncover insects.
facts.quote: They forage on the forest floor, flipping leaves to uncover insects; they may fly up to catch insects in flight.

facts.text: In one documented case, a wood thrush gave veery nestlings more care than the veery parents did.
facts.quote: However, a case of interspecific parental care of a veery nest by a wood thrush has been documented in which a wood thrush provided more parental care to the veery nestlings than did the parents, possibly due to sexual solicitation by the female veery.

facts.text: The veery got its name from its most common call, a harsh, descending vee-er.
facts.quote: The most common call is a harsh, descending vee-er, which gave the bird its name.

facts.text: Veery nests have been documented using parts of 27 plant species, including invasive ones.
facts.quote: The use of different parts of 27 plant species, including invasive/alien plants, has been documented, and nests in exotic plants appear to have similar reproductive success to those in native plants.

facts.text: The hermit thrush's song uses pitch ratios like those in human music, unlike other bird songs that have been analyzed the same way.
facts.quote: Analysis of the notes of its song indicates that they are related by harmonic simple integer pitch ratios, like many kinds of human music and unlike the songs of other birds that have been similarly examined.

facts.text: One description of the hermit thrush's song calls it "the finest sound in nature."
facts.quote: The hermit thrush's song has been described as "the finest sound in nature" and is ethereal and flute-like, consisting of a beginning note, then several descending musical phrases in a minor key, repeated at different pitches.

facts.text: Over the years, authors gave this bird 17 additional species or subspecies names, and all of them are now treated as synonyms.
facts.quote: The specific name guttatus is Latin for "spotted", though historically this species has been given 17 additional species or subspecies names by various authors, now all treated as synonyms.

facts.text: The Canadian indie-rock band Thrush Hermit got its name by reversing the bird's name.
facts.quote: Former Canadian indie-rock band Thrush Hermit took their name from a reversal of the bird's name.

facts.text: Of all the American spotted thrushes, the gray-cheeked thrush breeds farthest north.
facts.quote: Of all the American spotted thrushes, the gray-cheeked has the most northern breeding range.

facts.text: Gray-cheeked thrushes are believed to winter in the Amazon basin, crossing the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico during spring migration.
facts.quote: They are believed to spend their winter in the Amazon basin and will cross the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico during their spring migration.

facts.text: You're more likely to hear this thrush's nocturnal flight call during migration than to spot the bird on the ground.
facts.quote: It is more likely to hear its nocturnal flight call during spring and fall migration than to observe the species on the ground.

facts.text: Besides insects and berries, this thrush also eats crayfish, sow bugs, and earthworms.
facts.quote: It also feeds on crayfish, sow bugs, and earthworms.

facts.text: The female builds the nest from dried grasses mixed with a supporting layer of mud.
facts.quote: Females build the nest with dried grasses mixed with a supporting layer of mud.

facts.text: Local tribes say the Swainson's thrush's song makes salmonberries ripen, which is how it got the nickname "salmonberry bird."
facts.quote: Its song is said by local tribes to make salmonberries ripen, including the Saanich people who claim the bird says, "xwexwelexwelexwelexwesh!" meaning "ripen, ripen, ripen, ripen!"

facts.text: Swainson's thrushes in New Hampshire's White Mountains eat different insects depending on how high up they live.
facts.quote: A study in the White Mountains of New Hampshire found that Swainson's thrushes eat different insects depending on their elevation, with detritivores, particularly woodlice and ghost spiders, making up more of their diet at higher elevations.

facts.text: Its song is a hurried series of flute-like tones spiraling upward.
facts.quote: This bird's song is a hurried series of flute-like tones spiralling upwards.

facts.text: Swainson's thrush is the most ancient North American species of its genus, and it looks like its relatives because of convergent evolution.
facts.quote: These results notwithstanding, analysis of mtDNA cytochrome b and NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 as well as nuclear β-fibrinogen intron 7 sequence data shows that Swainson's thrush is the most ancient North American species of its genus; it is not closely related to other Catharus and the outward similarities with the other North American species are due to convergent evolution.

facts.text: Brown creepers zig-zag up a tree trunk, then fly down to the bottom of another tree.
facts.quote: Brown creepers forage on tree trunks and branches, typically zig-zagging upwards from the bottom of a tree trunk, and then flying down to the bottom of another tree.

facts.text: A female brown creeper builds a partial cup nest under a loose piece of bark or in a tree cavity.
facts.quote: The female will make a partial cup nest either under a piece of bark partially detached from the tree, or in a tree cavity.

facts.text: Brown creepers are hard to count because they avoid edges, blend in with bark, and have very high-pitched voices.
facts.quote: This species's avoidance of edges, cryptic plumage, and high-pitched vocalizations contribute to a low survey detection rate compared to other species.

facts.text: In El Salvador, brown creepers have been recorded breeding in January and February, which is unusual for insect-eating birds.
facts.quote: Brown creepers have been recorded breeding in the dry season (January–February) in Chalatenango Department, El Salvador, a behaviour unusual to insectivorous birds and shared in the region only by the golden-fronted woodpecker.

facts.text: In California's San Bernardino Mountains, creeper songs run up to thirteen syllables but fit in the same two seconds.
facts.quote: Creepers in California have songs of four to nine syllables, except in the San Bernardino Mountains, where there are as many as nine to thirteen syllables per song, but within the same two second time frame.

facts.text: Scientists learned where chimney swifts spend the winter in 1944, when bird bands turned up in Peru, worn as a necklace.
facts.quote: The chimney swift's wintering grounds were only discovered in 1944, when bands from birds banded (ringed) in North America were recovered in Peru. An indigenous Peruvian had been wearing the bands as a necklace.

facts.text: Chimney swifts bathe in flight, smacking their breast into the water and flying off, shaking their feathers as they go.
facts.quote: It drinks on the wing, skimming the surface of the water with its beak. It also bathes on the wing, gliding above the surface of a body of water, briefly smacking its breast into the water, then flying off again, shaking its feathers as it goes.

facts.text: Chimney swifts glue their stick nests together with saliva, and their salivary glands more than double in size when breeding.
facts.quote: The sticks are glued together (and the nest to a vertical surface) with copious amounts of the bird's saliva. During the breeding season, each adult's salivary glands more than double in size, from 7 mm × 2 mm (0.276 in × 0.079 in) in the non-breeding season to 14 mm × 5 mm (0.55 in × 0.20 in) during the breeding season.

facts.text: Hurricane Wilma in 2005 swept chimney swifts as far as Western Europe, with six reaching Great Britain.
facts.quote: Chimney swifts caught up in 2005's Hurricane Wilma were swept as far north as Atlantic Canada and Western Europe, including six reaching Great Britain, the most ever seen there in a single year.

facts.text: Disturbed chimney swifts clap their wings against their bodies, and a big roost can make a loud thundering sound.
facts.quote: If it is disturbed while at rest, the chimney swift will clap its wings loudly once or twice against its body; it does this either in place, or while dropping down several feet to a lower location. This behavior can result in a loud "thundering" sound if large roosts of the birds are disturbed.

facts.text: The semipalmated plover gets its name from its feet, which are only partly webbed.
facts.quote: The specific semipalmatus is  Latin and comes from  semi, "half" and palma, "palm". Like the English name, this refers to its only partially webbed feet.

facts.text: To lure intruders away from its ground nest, this plover puts on a "broken-wing" act, much like the killdeer.
facts.quote: Since the semipalmated plover nests on the ground, it uses a "broken-wing" display to lure intruders away from the nest, in a display similar to the related killdeer.

facts.text: Birders have found semipalmated plovers in Tierra del Fuego and the Isles of Scilly, far from their usual range.
facts.quote: They are extremely rare vagrants to western Europe, and have been found in Tierra del Fuego and the Isles of Scilly.

facts.text: The semipalmated plover used to be considered a subspecies of the ringed plover of Eurasia.
facts.quote: Their true status may be obscured by the difficulty in identifying them from the very similar ringed plover of Eurasia, of which it was formerly considered a subspecies.

facts.text: Semipalmated plovers mostly hunt by sight, and their menu includes insects, spiders, worms, snails and berries.
facts.quote: Semipalmated plovers forage for food on beaches, tidal flats and fields, usually by sight. They eat insects (such as the larvae of long-legged and beach flies, larvae of soldier flies and shore flies, mosquitoes, grasshoppers and Ochtebius beetles), spiders, crustaceans (such as isopods, decapods and copepods) and worms (such as polychaetes).

facts.text: Killdeer are shorebirds, but they don't necessarily nest near water, and they sometimes nest on rooftops.
facts.quote: Its breeding grounds are generally open fields with short vegetation (but locations such as rooftops are sometimes used); although it is a shorebird, it does not necessarily nest close to water.

facts.text: In the nonbreeding season, killdeer feed more at night and roost more during the day when the moon is full.
facts.quote: During the nonbreeding season, the killdeer forages during the night, depending on the lunar cycle. When the moon is full, it feeds more at night and roosts more during the day.

facts.text: Killdeer sometimes follow plows in fields to grab earthworms that get turned up to the surface.
facts.quote: When feeding in fields, it sometimes follows plows to take earthworms disturbed to the surface.

facts.text: To find food, a killdeer may stand on one foot and shake the other in shallow water for about five seconds, pecking at stirred-up prey.
facts.quote: An example of this is "foot-trembling", where it stands on one foot, shaking the other in shallow water for about five seconds, pecking at any prey stirred up.

facts.text: In its ungulate display, a killdeer charges at an intruder with raised wings, which can be fatal to the bird.
facts.quote: Another behavior that has received attention is the "ungulate display", where the adult raises its wings, exposes its rump, lowers its head, and charges at the intruder. This can be fatal to the displaying bird.

facts.text: Its "bull-bat" nickname comes from its bat-like flight and the bull-like boom its wings make when pulling out of a dive.
facts.quote: The common nighthawk is sometimes called a "bull-bat", due to its perceived "bat-like" flight, and the "bull-like" boom made by its wings as it pulls from a dive.

facts.text: Nighthawks don't build nests; the eggs are laid on bare rock, gravel, or sometimes on lichen.
facts.quote: The eggs are not laid in a nest, but on bare rock, gravel, or sometimes a living substrate such as lichen.

facts.text: Until the early 19th century, people thought the common nighthawk and the whip-poor-will were one species.
facts.quote: Up until the early 19th century, the common nighthawk and the whip-poor-will were thought to be one species.

facts.text: Nebraska's old nickname, the "Bugeater State," likely came from the common nighthawk.
facts.quote: The common nighthawk is likely the reason that Nebraska's state nickname was once the "Bugeater State", and its people were known as "bugeaters".

facts.text: After chicks hatch, the mother may carry the eggshells elsewhere or eat part of them, since leftover debris can attract predators.
facts.quote: Once the chicks have broken out of the shells, the removal of the debris is necessary in order to avoid predators. The mother may carry the eggshells to another location or consume a portion of them.

facts.text: A male marsh wren builds many unused nests in his territory.
facts.quote: The male builds many unused nests in his territory.

facts.text: A male marsh wren may puncture eggs and fatally peck nestlings nearby, even his own offspring.
facts.quote: He may puncture the eggs and fatally peck the nestlings of other birds nesting nearby, including his own species (even his own offspring) and red-winged blackbirds, yellow-headed blackbirds, and least bitterns.

facts.text: Marsh wren eggs can withstand pressure 2.9 times higher than expected compared with other passerine eggs.
facts.quote: Likely because of this, marsh wren eggs are able to withstand pressure 2.9 times higher than expected when compared to eggs from other passerine species.

facts.text: Abandoned marsh wren nests may be used by other animals, including meadow jumping mice.
facts.quote: Abandoned marsh wren nests may also be used by other animals, including meadow jumping mouse.

facts.text: The marsh wren was once called the long-billed marsh wren to tell it apart from the sedge wren, then called the short-billed marsh wren.
facts.quote: It was formerly called the long-billed marsh wren to distinguish it from the sedge wren, then known as the short-billed marsh wren.

facts.text: Sedge wrens improvise their songs instead of learning them from other birds.
facts.quote: Sedge wrens improvise their songs rather than learning them from other birds.

facts.text: Male sedge wrens build multiple nests, and some serve as dormitories or as decoys to fool predators.
facts.quote: Males are also the ones building the nests. They build multiple nests which serve for nesting, as dormitories and as decoys for predators.

facts.text: Male sedge wrens sing both during the day and at night.
facts.quote: Males sing from late winter to early spring on non-breeding grounds and throughout the breeding season to attract mates. They sing both during the day and the night.

facts.text: In a singing duel, a male sedge wren usually answers a rival male with a different song type.
facts.quote: A male will usually answer the other male with a different song type and frequently change song types during the interaction.

facts.text: The sedge wren used to be called the short-billed marsh wren until it was renamed to set it apart from the marsh wren.
facts.quote: The sedge wren was formerly known as the short-billed marsh wren but was renamed to better distinguish it from the marsh wren.

facts.text: In the southern U.S., this bird is nicknamed the rain crow and storm crow, likely because it calls on hot days before showers or storms.
facts.quote: Common folk names for this bird in the southern United States are rain crow and storm crow. These likely refer to the bird's habit of calling on hot days, often presaging rain showers or thunderstorms.

facts.text: Around 75% of yellow-billed cuckoos travel an average of 965 km between two sites during the breeding season.
facts.quote: Around 75% of cuckoos will travel an average of 965 km between two sites during the breeding season, likely in order to take advantage of changing resource availability at different sites and raise two successive broods of eggs.

facts.text: From egg-laying to fledging can take as little as 17 days for a yellow-billed cuckoo.
facts.quote: The entire time from egg-laying to fledging may be as little as 17 days.

facts.text: They mainly eat insects, especially tent caterpillars and cicadas, but also some lizards, eggs of other birds, and berries.
facts.quote: They mainly eat insects, especially tent caterpillars and cicadas, but also some lizards, eggs of other birds, and berries.

facts.text: Yellow-billed cuckoos occasionally lay eggs in other birds' nests, most often those of the closely related black-billed cuckoo.
facts.quote: Yellow-billed cuckoos occasionally lay eggs in the nests of other birds (most often the closely related black-billed cuckoo), but they are not obligate brood parasites of other birds as is the common cuckoo of Eurasia.

facts.text: A flicker's tongue can dart out 2 inches beyond the end of its bill to catch prey.
facts.quote: Their tongues can dart out 50 mm (2 in) beyond the end of the bill to catch prey.

facts.text: Flickers have been seen breaking up cow dung to eat the insects living inside it.
facts.quote: They have been observed breaking up cow dung to eat the insects living within.

facts.text: Flickers hammer at the soil to break into underground ant colonies and reach the nutritious larvae.
facts.quote: Northern flickers often break into underground ant colonies to get at the nutritious larvae there, hammering at the soil the way other woodpeckers drill into wood.

facts.text: Northern flickers have over 100 known common names, including wake-up, walk-up and gawker bird.
facts.quote: Over 100 common names for the northern flicker are known, including yellowhammer (not to be confused with the Eurasian yellowhammer (Emberiza citrinella)), clape, gaffer woodpecker, harry-wicket, heigh-ho, wake-up, walk-up, wick-up, yarrup, and gawker bird.

facts.text: Flickers use formic acid from ants while preening, which helps keep parasites away.
facts.quote: As well as eating ants, northern flickers exhibit a behavior known as anting, in which they use the formic acid from the ants to assist in preening, as it is useful in keeping them free of parasites.

facts.text: Pigeons can dip their bills in water and drink continuously, without tilting their heads back the way most birds do.
facts.quote: While most birds take small sips and tilt their heads backwards when drinking, pigeons are able to dip their bills into the water and drink continuously, without having to tilt their heads back.

facts.text: Because they can produce crop milk, rock doves can breed at any time of the year.
facts.quote: The species can breed at any time of the year due to their ability to produce crop milk, but peak times are spring and summer, when the food supply is abundant enough to support embryonic egg development.

facts.text: Rock doves were central to Charles Darwin's discovery of evolution and appeared in four of his works.
facts.quote: The rock dove was central to Charles Darwin's discovery of evolution, and featured in four of his works from 1859 to 1872.

facts.text: When a predator grabs a pigeon, loose feathers often come off in its mouth, which may give the pigeon a chance to escape.
facts.quote: When a predator catches a pigeon, large numbers of feathers are often pulled by the attacker's mouth and the pigeon may use this temporary distraction to make an escape.

facts.text: Rock doves stamp one foot first, showing a "footedness" similar to human handedness.
facts.quote: Foot stamping is done with a certain foot first, showing that rock doves have "footedness", similar to human handedness.

facts.text: Eastern wood pewees build their nests on a horizontal tree branch and use spider webs to hold them there.
facts.quote: The eastern wood pewee makes an open cup nest made of grasses, bark, and lichen, attached to a horizontal tree branch with spider webs.

facts.text: Male eastern wood pewees guard their nesting area aggressively, even attacking robins and chipping sparrows.
facts.quote: Males are territorial and defend the nesting area aggressively, often fighting with neighbouring conspecifics and even pursue attacks on other species (e.g., least flycatchers, American robins, chipping sparrows, red-eyed vireos, etc.).

facts.text: A young eastern wood pewee often lands on the ground on its first flight out of the nest.
facts.quote: Nestlings typically fledge 15–17 days after hatching, often ending up on the ground during the first flight out of the nest.

facts.text: The eastern wood pewee gets its name from its mournful whistled song, pee-a'wee.
facts.quote: The songs are basically a mournful whistled pee-a'wee given in a series, which gave this bird its name, and a "pe-wee" with a rising note at the end.

facts.text: Eastern and western wood pewees look virtually identical, so birders tell them apart most easily by their calls.
facts.quote: The two species are virtually identical in appearance, and can be distinguished most easily by their calls.

facts.text: A ruby-crowned kinglet can lay up to 12 eggs, the largest clutch of any North American passerine for its size.
facts.quote: It lays up to 12 eggs, and has the largest clutch of any North American passerine for its size.

facts.text: Ruby-crowned kinglets often fake a broken wing to lure predators from the nest, and they mob intruders like cats, squirrels, or humans.
facts.quote: Often, they perform a "broken-wing" act to draw predators away from their nest, which they will defend fearlessly, mobbing the intruder which may be a cat, squirrel, or human.

facts.text: For such a tiny bird, the ruby-crowned kinglet has a remarkably loud and complex voice.
facts.quote: The ruby-crowned kinglet's vocalizations are remarkably loud and complex for its size.

facts.text: A Guadalupe Island form of the ruby-crowned kinglet was last sighted in 1953 and is considered extinct.
facts.quote: The subspecies C. c. obscurus, from Guadalupe Island, off Baja California, was last sighted in 1953 and is considered extinct.

facts.text: Ruby-crowned kinglets may hover over a branch while feeding and sometimes fly out to catch insects in flight.
facts.quote: They may hover over a branch while feeding and sometimes fly out to catch insects in flight.

facts.text: In one example, a crow pecked a river otter's tail to distract it while other crows swooped in and stole its fish.
facts.quote: One example shows a group of crows stealing a fish from a Northern river otter: one bird pecked the otter's tail to distract it while other birds swooped in and stole the fish.

facts.text: Crows have been noted at play, including snowboarding using tree bark.
facts.quote: American crows have also been noted for their ability to play, such as snowboarding using tree bark.

facts.text: Outside nesting season, crows often gather at night in communal roosts of thousands or even millions of birds.
facts.quote: Outside the nesting season, these birds often gather in large communal roosts of thousands or even millions of crows at night.

facts.text: Crows can remember and identify people based on their appearance.
facts.quote: They can remember and identify people based on their appearance.

facts.text: American crows sometimes mimic noises made by other animals, including barred owls.
facts.quote: American crows can also produce a wide variety of sounds and sometimes mimic noises made by other animals, including other birds, such as barred owls.

facts.text: When one raven in a mated pair is lost, its mate copies the lost partner's calls to encourage it to return.
facts.quote: If a member of a pair is lost, its mate reproduces the calls of its lost partner to encourage its return.

facts.text: Ravens have been seen dropping stones on potential predators that venture close to their nests.
facts.quote: They have been observed dropping stones on potential predators that venture close to their nests.

facts.text: Ravens have been seen pretending to hide food without leaving any, presumably to confuse onlookers.
facts.quote: They have also been observed pretending to make a cache without actually depositing the food, presumably to confuse onlookers.

facts.text: Ravens have been observed leading hunting wolf packs to prey that only the ravens can see from the air.
facts.quote: They often associate with another canine, the wolf, as a kleptoparasite, following to scavenge wolf-kills in winter, but also co-operatively, having been observed to lead hunting wolf packs to potential prey that only the ravens can see from the air.

facts.text: Young ravens are among the most playful birds and have been seen sliding down snowbanks, apparently purely for fun.
facts.quote: Juvenile common ravens are among the most playful of bird species. They have been observed to slide down snowbanks, apparently purely for fun.

facts.text: Blue jays can copy the cries of local hawks so well that it can be hard to tell which bird you're hearing.
facts.quote: Blue jays can also copy the cries of local hawks so well that it is sometimes difficult to tell which it is.

facts.text: One blue jay call is nicknamed the "rusty pump" because it squeaks like an old hand-operated water pump.
facts.quote: One of the most distinctive calls of this type is often referred to as the "rusty pump" owing to its squeaky resemblance to the sound of an old hand-operated water pump.

facts.text: Young blue jays playfully snatch bottle caps and aluminum foil and carry them around until they lose interest.
facts.quote: Young individuals playfully snatch brightly colored or reflective objects, such as bottle caps or pieces of aluminum foil, and carry them around until they lose interest.

facts.text: The oldest known wild, banded blue jay lived at least 26 years and 11 months.
facts.quote: The oldest known wild, banded blue jay was at least 26 years, 11 months old when it was found dead after being caught in fishing gear.

facts.text: If no better spot is available, blue jays will even use the large mailboxes typical of the rural United States.
facts.quote: If no better place is available – such as in a heavily deforested area – they will even use places like the large mailboxes typical of the rural United States.

facts.text: Male trumpeter swans build nests by facing away and throwing material over their shoulders, moving closer and closer to the nest site.
facts.quote: The males use a specific action that includes facing away from the nest and throwing organic materials over their shoulder moving closer and closer to the nesting area.

facts.text: While sitting on eggs, a female stands up about every 20 minutes and rolls them over with her bill.
facts.quote: It has been observed that around every 20 minutes the female will stand up from incubating and reach down beneath herself to roll over the eggs with her bill before re-assuming the incubation position.

facts.text: By 1933, fewer than 70 wild trumpeters were known, until aerial surveys found several thousand around Alaska's Copper River.
facts.quote: By 1933, fewer than 70 wild individuals were known to exist; extinction seemed imminent until aerial surveys discovered a Pacific population of several thousand trumpeter swans around Alaska's Copper River.

facts.text: A mated pair's trumpeting can start as separate solos and blend into a near-simultaneous duet that is hard to tell apart.
facts.quote: The duetting process can begin as separate trumpeting solos and can evolve into an almost simultaneous duet that is very similar in frequency and very difficult to tell the individual calls apart.

facts.text: Trumpeter swan parents have beaten predators equal to their own weight, such as coyotes, in confrontations.
facts.quote: Adults have managed to beat predators equal to their own weight such as coyotes in confrontations.

facts.text: One tracked bobolink flew 12,000 miles in a year, sometimes covering up to 1,100 miles in a single day before resting for days or weeks.
facts.quote: One bird was tracked migrating 12,000 mi (19,000 km) over the course of the year, often flying long distances up to 1,100 mi (1,800 km) in a single day, then stopping to recuperate for days or weeks.

facts.text: In Jamaica, bobolinks are called "butter-birds" because they were collected as food after fattening up on rice.
facts.quote: One of the species' main migration routes is through Jamaica, where they are called "butter-birds" and at least historically were collected as food, having fattened up on the aforementioned rice.

facts.text: Charles Darwin collected a bobolink in the Galápagos Islands in 1835.
facts.quote: A bobolink was collected in the Galápagos Islands by Charles Darwin in 1835.

facts.text: Bobolinks are nicknamed the "armyworm bird" because they eat large numbers of armyworms, acting as natural pest control.
facts.quote: They are nicknamed the "armyworm bird" because of their predation on large numbers of armyworms, including the true armyworm (Mythimna unipuncta) and the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda), acting as a natural pest control.

facts.text: The bobolink's English name comes from "Bob o' Lincoln," which describes its call.
facts.quote: The English name "bobolink" is from Bob o' Lincoln, describing the call.

facts.text: Downy woodpeckers prey on the European corn borer, an invasive moth costing US agriculture over $1 billion a year.
facts.quote: They are a natural predator of the European corn borer, an invasive moth that costs the US agriculture industry more than $1 billion annually in crop losses and population control.

facts.text: The downy woodpecker's rattle call is a short burst that sounds similar to a bouncing ball.
facts.quote: The rattle-call is a short burst that sounds similar to a bouncing ball, while that of the hairy woodpecker is a shorter burst of the same amplitude.

facts.text: Building a downy woodpecker nest hole takes about two or three weeks.
facts.quote: The nest hole takes about two or three weeks to create, and normally measures 12 to 15 cm wide and about 20 to 30 cm deep.

facts.text: Downy woodpecker parents take turns warming the eggs by day, and the male typically takes the night shift.
facts.quote: During waking hours, both birds will incubate, or warm the eggs for 15 minute periods, taking turns in alternating shifts. At night, the male woodpecker typically will rest on the eggs for their continued warmth.

facts.text: Downy and hairy woodpeckers look alike but are not very closely related; the resemblance is convergent evolution.
facts.quote: Despite their close resemblance, the downy and hairy woodpeckers are not very closely related; the outward similarity is an example of convergent evolution.

facts.text: An English naturalist, Mark Catesby, described and drew this bird on a hand-colored plate in a book published between 1729 and 1732.
facts.quote: The hairy woodpecker was described and illustrated with a hand-coloured plate by the English naturalist Mark Catesby in his The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands which was published between 1729 and 1732.

facts.text: Hairy woodpeckers prey on the European corn borer, an invasive moth that costs US agriculture over $1 billion a year.
facts.quote: They are a predator of the European corn borer, an invasive moth that costs the US agriculture industry more than $1 billion annually in crop losses and population control.

facts.text: The hairy woodpecker looks almost identical to the downy woodpecker, yet the two are not closely related.
facts.quote: It is virtually identical in plumage to the smaller downy woodpecker. The downy has a shorter bill relative to the size of its head, which is, other than size and voice, the best way to distinguish them in the field.  These two species are not closely related, however.

facts.text: Hairy woodpecker pairs dig a hole in a tree and lay, on average, four white eggs inside.
facts.quote: Mating pairs will excavate a hole in a tree, where they will lay, on average, four white eggs.

facts.text: Besides insects, hairy woodpeckers also eat fruits, berries, nuts and sometimes tree sap.
facts.quote: They mainly eat insects, but also fruits, berries and nuts, as well as sometimes tree sap.

facts.text: Once pileated woodpeckers find a mate, they typically stay together for life.
facts.quote: Once the birds have found a mate, they typically stay together for life.

facts.text: Woodpeckers can make holes in dead trees so large that a small tree breaks in half.
facts.quote: Woodpeckers make such large holes in dead trees that the holes can cause a small tree to break in half.

facts.text: A pileated woodpecker may move to a new nest site if an egg falls out, a rare habit in birds.
facts.quote: Pileated woodpeckers may also move to another site if any eggs have fallen out of the nest—a rare habit in birds.

facts.text: Pileated woodpeckers often drum on hollow trees to make the most resonant sound possible when proclaiming territory.
facts.quote: Drumming is used to proclaim territory, and they often do this on hollow trees to make the most resonant sound possible.

facts.text: Woody Woodpecker's look is believed to come from the pileated woodpecker, but his call was patterned on the acorn woodpecker.
facts.quote: Cartoonist Walter Lantz is believed to have based the appearance of his creation Woody Woodpecker on the pileated woodpecker; while patterning the call on the acorn woodpecker.

facts.text: A catbird can make two sounds at the same time thanks to its well-developed songbird syrinx.
facts.quote: Because of its well-developed songbird syrinx, it is able to make two sounds at the same time.

facts.text: Catbirds peck and destroy the eggs that brown-headed cowbirds lay in their nests.
facts.quote: They also will destroy eggs of the brood parasitic brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater) laid in their nests by pecking them.

facts.text: Besides birdsong, catbirds mimic tree frogs and even mechanical sounds.
facts.quote: Like many members of the Mimidae (in particular mockingbirds), it also mimics the songs of other birds, as well as those of Hylidae (tree frogs), and even mechanical sounds.

facts.text: Unlike many songbirds, the catbird often sings from inside a bush or small tree, hidden by the leaves.
facts.quote: In contrast to the many songbirds that choose a prominent perch from which to sing, the catbird often elects to sing from inside a bush or small tree, where it is obscured from view by the foliage.

facts.text: The least flycatcher's nickname, chebec, comes from the sound the bird makes.
facts.quote: The least flycatcher (Empidonax minimus) (also called chebec, or chebecker, after the sound it makes) is a small insect-eating bird.

facts.text: One study found that least flycatchers go after 81.1% of their prey by hovering.
facts.quote: In short, Robinson and Holmes (1982) determined that the least flycatcher attacks 81.1% of their preys by hovering, 9.6% by hawking, 6.2% by flush-chasing and 3.1% by gleaning.

facts.text: Willow and alder flycatchers were once counted as one species, and song is the only reliable way to tell them apart in the field.
facts.quote: At one time, this bird and the alder flycatcher (Empidonax alnorum) were considered to be a single species, Traill's flycatcher. Their song is the only reliable method to tell them apart in the field.

facts.text: The willow flycatcher's song is a sneezed "fitz-bew."
facts.quote: This bird's song is a sneezed fitz-bew.

facts.text: Audubon chose the species name traillii to honor his friend Thomas Stewart Traill, a Scottish physician and zoologist.
facts.quote: The specific epithet was chosen by Audubon to honour his friend the Scottish physician and zoologist Thomas Stewart Traill.

facts.text: Willow flycatchers travel approximately 1,500 to 8,000 km each way between their winter and breeding areas.
facts.quote: Willow flycatchers travel approximately 1,500–8,000 km (930–4,970 mi) each way between wintering and breeding areas.

facts.text: Willow flycatchers are "sit-and-wait" hunters that perch near the top of a shrub and fly out to catch insects on the wing.
facts.quote: They are "sit-and-wait" predators, remaining on a perch near the top of a shrub and flying out to catch insects on the wing, but are also reported to glean insects off of leaves and stems.

facts.text: Despite its name, the Acadian flycatcher has no native range in Acadia; the name came from a misidentified specimen collected there.
facts.quote: Because of the similar appearance of the Empidonax flycatchers, the Acadian flycatcher owes its name to a misidentified type specimen for the species, taken in the historic Acadia region of Nova Scotia. Despite its common name, the Acadian flycatcher does not have a native range in Nova Scotia or historic Acadia.

facts.text: Cowbirds lay eggs in Acadian flycatcher nests, but only 16% of the cowbird young there fledge successfully.
facts.quote: Brown-headed cowbirds lay eggs in the nests of these birds in some areas. However, only 16% of cowbird young in Acadian flycatcher nests fledge successfully.

facts.text: This flycatcher can hover and even fly backwards for short stretches.
facts.quote: The bird is quick and direct with its movements, capable of hovering and flying backwards for short durations.

facts.text: It waits on a perch, then flies out to snatch insects in midair, a move called hawking.
facts.quote: They wait on a perch in the middle of a tree and fly out to catch insects in flight (hawking), also sometimes picking insects from foliage while hovering (gleaning).

facts.text: A flycatcher found on a beach in Kent, England, in 2015 was identified by DNA from its droppings.
facts.quote: As of October 2015 there have been 2 records of Acadian flycatcher in Europe, the first being a bird found dead in Iceland in 1967, and the second a bird found on the beach at Dungeness in Kent, England in September 2015, the latter's identity being established by DNA from its droppings.

facts.text: A courting male sings while circling above the female, then dives with folded wings and opens them just before reaching the ground.
facts.quote: Courting involves the male singing to the female while flying above her in circles. He then will fold his wings in and dive towards the female, opening his wings just before reaching the ground.

facts.text: Females often add a "doorstep" of pebbles, corncobs, or dung to one side of the nest.
facts.quote: It has been noted that she often adds a "doorstep" of pebbles, corncobs, or dung on one side of the nest.

facts.text: In 2020, a well-preserved frozen horned lark was found in Siberian permafrost in the Russian Far East.
facts.quote: In 2020, a well-preserved, complete frozen bird carcass of a female horned lark was discovered in Siberian permafrost from the Russian Far East.

facts.text: A female horned lark may dig her own nest cavity in the ground using her bill and feet.
facts.quote: The nest site is selected in the early spring by only the female and is either a natural depression in the bare ground or she digs a cavity using her bill and feet.

facts.text: Female horned larks sometimes line their nests with lint, along with down, fur, and feathers.
facts.quote: She weaves fine grasses, cornstalks, small roots, and other plant material and lines it with down, fur, feathers, and occasionally lint.

facts.text: Emerging dragonflies and their larvae are an important summer food for rusty blackbirds.
facts.quote: Emerging dragonflies and their larvae are important food items during the summer.

facts.text: Rusty blackbirds usually nest at the edge of ponds and wetlands, often building their cup nest over the water.
facts.quote: Birds usually nest at the edge of ponds and wetlands with the cup nest located in a tree or dense shrub, often over the water.

facts.text: The rusty blackbird's song is a mix of gurgling and high-pitched squeaks, and both males and females sing it.
facts.quote: Fairly quiet in fall migration and most of the winter, both males and females will sing (particularly on warm days) in the late winter and spring. The song consists of gurgling and high-pitched squeaks.

facts.text: Rusty blackbirds migrate slowly in autumn, often staying in the northern states well into December, but spring migration is much faster.
facts.quote: Their autumn migration is slow, with birds often remaining in the northern states well into December; spring migration is much more rapid.

facts.text: In the Cayman Islands, bananaquits were noted to die of an apparent heart attack or stroke when a merlin went at them.
facts.quote: In the Cayman Islands (where it only occurs in winter), bananaquits were noted to die of an apparent heart attack or stroke, without being physically harmed, when a merlin went at them and they could not escape.

facts.text: Merlins have even been observed trying to "catch" cars and trains.
facts.quote: Merlins have even been observed trying to "catch" automobiles and trains and to feed on captive birds such as those snared in the mist nets used by ornithologists.

facts.text: Merlins don't build a proper nest of their own; most use abandoned crow, magpie or hawk nests.
facts.quote: Most nest sites have dense vegetative or rocky cover; the merlin does not build a proper nest of its own. Most will use abandoned corvid (particularly Corvus crow and Pica magpie) or hawk nests which are in conifer or mixed tree stands.

facts.text: The falcon's name has no historical connection to the Arthurian wizard Merlin, despite the identical spelling and pronunciation.
facts.quote: Despite the identical spelling and pronunciation, the falcon’s name bears absolutely no historical or etymological connection to the legendary Arthurian wizard Merlin.

facts.text: Merlins are so eager to drive larger raptors from their territory that it helps identify them.
facts.quote: Their desire to drive larger raptors away from their territory is so pronounced that it is an identifying characteristic.

facts.text: The black spots on a kestrel's nape are most commonly thought to act as "false eyes" that help protect it from attackers.
facts.quote: The function of these spots is debated, but the most commonly accepted theory is that they act as "false eyes", and help to protect the bird from potential attackers.

facts.text: Kestrels are nicknamed "grasshopper hawk" for their diet and "killy hawk" for their distinct call.
facts.quote: Several other colloquial names for the kestrel are also in use, including grasshopper hawk, due to its diet, and killy hawk, due to its distinct call.

facts.text: Male kestrels attract mates with dive displays of several climbs and dives, calling "klee" three or four times at the peaks.
facts.quote: Males perform elaborate dive displays to advertise their territory and attract a mate. These displays consist of several climbs and dives, with three or four "klee" calls at their peaks.

facts.text: Baby kestrels can make calls similar to those of adults by the time they are 16 days old.
facts.quote: Nestlings can produce calls similar to those of adults at 16 days old.

facts.text: If catching prey gets significantly harder in one spot, a kestrel will move to hunt in a different area.
facts.quote: For example, if the success rate for catching prey decreases significantly in a particular area, the bird will move to a different area.

facts.text: Loon chicks can make shallow dives from their first day of life.
facts.quote: The chicks are capable of making shallow dives from their first day but make deeper dives as they grow.

facts.text: A loon is clumsy on land because its legs sit at the rear of its body, which is great for swimming but poor for walking.
facts.quote: Its clumsiness on land is due to the legs being positioned at the rear of its body; the pelvic muscles are well developed, ideal for swimming but not well-suited for walking.

facts.text: Unlike most flying birds, loons have a number of solid bones, which add weight but help them dive.
facts.quote: It has a skeletal structure made up of a number of solid bones (this is usual for the Gaviiformes and penguins but unlike most flying birds which have bones with extensive pneumatization, hollow and filled with air to make the skeleton lighter), which adds weight but helps in diving.

facts.text: A loon pair raising two chicks is estimated to eat 423 kilograms of fish during five and a half months on their territory.
facts.quote: A pair of loons raising two chicks have been estimated to feed on 423 kilograms (933 lb) of fish during the five and a half months that they spend in their breeding territory.

facts.text: The common loon appears on Canada's one-dollar "loonie" coin.
facts.quote: The common loon is the provincial bird of Ontario, and it appears on Canadian currency, including the one-dollar "loonie" coin and a previous series of $20 bills.

facts.text: Common yellowthroats were once also known as the "yellow bandit."
facts.quote: Historically, it has also been known as the "yellow bandit", Maryland yellow-throat, and yellow-breasted warbler.

facts.text: Female common yellowthroats appear to prefer males with larger masks.
facts.quote: Females appear to prefer males with larger masks.

facts.text: Yellowthroats mostly catch insects in dense vegetation, but sometimes snatch them in midair.
facts.quote: These birds feed on insects, which are usually captured in dense vegetation, but sometimes caught in midair.

facts.text: Brown-headed cowbirds commonly parasitize common yellowthroat nests.
facts.quote: Common yellowthroat nests are commonly subject to brood parasitism by the brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater).

facts.text: In spring migration, male common yellowthroats generally arrive at their destination before the females.
facts.quote: However, males generally arrive at their destination site before the females during the spring migration months.

facts.text: Sold illegally in New York City as "Hollywood finches," house finches were released by vendors and owners to avoid prosecution.
facts.quote: The birds were sold illegally in New York City as "Hollywood finches", a marketing artifice. To avoid prosecution under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918, vendors and owners released the birds.

facts.text: House finches are one of the few birds that feed their nestlings only plant matter instead of animal matter.
facts.quote: Contrary to the way most birds, even ones with herbivorous leanings as adults, tend to feed their nestlings animal matter to give them the protein necessary to grow, house finches are one of the few birds who feed their young only plant matter.

facts.text: A mother house finch may lay female eggs first, since mites hurt male chicks more and this shortens their time exposed.
facts.quote: In response to mite infestation, which has a more deleterious effect on male chicks than on females, the mother finch may lay eggs containing females first, to reduce the length of time male chicks are exposed to mites.

facts.text: During courtship, a female house finch may act like a hungry chick, and the male may feed her.
facts.quote: He may then present the female with choice bits of food, and if she mimics the behavior of a hungry chick, he may feed her.

facts.text: A male house finch's color is derived from the berries and fruits in his diet.
facts.quote: Male coloration varies in intensity with the seasons and is derived from the berries and fruits in its diet.

facts.text: A bald eagle's nest can be 4 m deep and weigh 1 metric ton, the largest tree nest recorded for any animal.
facts.quote: It builds the largest nest of any North American bird and the largest tree nests ever recorded for any animal species, up to 4 m (13 ft) deep, 2.5 m (8.2 ft) wide, and 1 metric ton (1.1 short tons) in weight.

facts.text: A bald eagle can store up to 1 kg of food in a throat pouch called a crop, which lets it fast for several days.
facts.quote: When food is abundant, an eagle can gorge itself by storing up to 1 kg (2.2 lb) of food in a pouch in the throat called a crop. Gorging allows the bird to fast for several days if food becomes unavailable.

facts.text: A family of bald eagles moved into New York City's Harlem neighborhood in 2010.
facts.quote: Even more contrary to the usual sensitivity to disturbance, a family of bald eagles moved to the Harlem neighborhood in New York City in 2010.

facts.text: The "bald" in bald eagle comes from an older meaning of the word: "white-headed."
facts.quote: Bald eagles are not bald in the literal sense; the name derives from an older meaning of the word, "white-headed".

facts.text: A bald eagle's grip is estimated to be ten times stronger than a human's.
facts.quote: It has been estimated that the bald eagle's grip (measured as newtons per square meter, or pounds per square inch) is ten times stronger than that of a human.

facts.text: One barn swallow roost in Nigeria had an estimated 1.5 million birds.
facts.quote: These roosts can be extremely large; one in Nigeria had an estimated 1.5 million birds.

facts.text: In North America, barn swallows often nest below an osprey nest, protected from other birds of prey that the fish-eating ospreys repel.
facts.quote: In North America at least, barn swallows frequently engage in a mutualist relationship with ospreys. Barn swallows will build their nest below an osprey nest, receiving protection from other birds of prey that are repelled by the exclusively fish-eating ospreys.

facts.text: One barn swallow nest was reported to have been occupied for 48 years.
facts.quote: Survival, with suitable annual refurbishment, for 10–15 years is regular, and one nest was reported to have been occupied for 48 years.

facts.text: In Africa, tigerfish have been recorded routinely leaping out of the water to catch low-flying swallows.
facts.quote: In Africa, tigerfish Hydrocynus vittatus have been recorded to routinely leap out of the water to capture low-flying swallows.

facts.text: A swallow tattoo is a sailor's tradition, a symbol of a safe return, earned after sailing 5,000 nautical miles.
facts.quote: Elsewhere, its long journeys were well observed, and a swallow tattoo is traditional among sailors as a symbol of a safe return; the tradition was that a mariner had a tattoo of this fellow wanderer after sailing 5,000 nautical miles (9,300 kilometres).

facts.text: The Caspian tern's call is a loud croak that sounds like a heron's.
facts.quote: The call is a loud heron-like croak.

facts.text: In 2016, a pair bred successfully in northwestern Alaska, 600 km farther north than any earlier North American breeding record.
facts.quote: In 2016, a pair of Caspian terns bred successfully in the Cape Krusenstern National Monument in northwestern Alaska, 600 km further north than any previous North American breeding record.

facts.text: A Caspian tern may fly up to 60 km from its breeding colony to catch fish.
facts.quote: They may fly up to 60 km (37 mi) from the breeding colony to catch fish; they often fish on freshwater lakes as well as at sea.

facts.text: A male wood thrush can sing two notes at once, which gives its song a flute-like quality.
facts.quote: The male is able to sing two notes at once, which gives its song an ethereal, flute-like quality.

facts.text: Wood thrushes sometimes rub ants on their feathers, a habit called anting, and the purpose is unknown.
facts.quote: Anting occurs when a bird picks up a single ant or group of ants and rubs them on its feathers. The purpose of this behavior is unknown, but it is thought that the birds may be able to acquire defensive secretions from the ants possibly used for some medicinal purposes, or that it simply supplements the birds' own preen oil.

facts.text: Wood thrushes migrate at night, finding their direction from the stars and by detecting the Earth's magnetic field.
facts.quote: Migration takes place at night, allowing them to find their direction from the stars and orient themselves by detecting the Earth's magnetic field.

facts.text: Wood thrushes have turned up in Europe twice: in Iceland in 1967 and in England's Isles of Scilly in 1987.
facts.quote: The wood thrush has been recorded twice as a vagrant in Europe, in Iceland at Kvísker in Öræfi East Skaftafellssýsla by Björnsson Hálfdán on 23 October 1967 and on Wingletang Down, St Agnes, Isles of Scilly, England on 7 October 1987.

facts.text: The wood thrush's species name, mustelina, comes from the Latin word mustela, which means weasel.
facts.quote: The species name comes from the Latin mustela "weasel".
