facts.text: The Baltimore oriole's name comes from the male's colors resembling the coat-of-arms of 17th-century Lord Baltimore.
facts.quote: It received its common name from the resemblance of the male's colors to those on the coat-of-arms of 17th-century Lord Baltimore.

facts.text: Orioles beat caterpillars against a branch to strip off their protective hairs before eating them.
facts.quote: The larvae caterpillar is beaten against a branch until their protective hairs are skinned off before being eaten.

facts.text: Orioles seek out the darkest mulberries and deepest-purple grapes, and ignore green grapes and yellow cherries even when ripe.
facts.quote: Orioles seek out the darkest mulberries, the reddest cherries, and the deepest-purple grapes, and will ignore green grapes and yellow cherries even if they are ripe.

facts.text: If orioles discover a well-kept feeder, they lead their young there.
facts.quote: If they discover a well-kept feeder, orioles lead their young there.

facts.text: The oldest recorded wild Baltimore oriole lived to 11 years and 7 months.
facts.quote: The oldest recorded Baltimore oriole lived to 11 years and 7 months in the wild.

facts.text: A flock of dark-eyed juncos has been known to be called a blizzard.
facts.quote: A flock of dark-eyed juncos has been known to be called a blizzard.

facts.text: Juncos on the UC San Diego campus can raise as many as four broods per year, rather than the one or two of nearby populations.
facts.quote: This allows UCSD juncos to have as many as four broods per year, rather than the one or two of nearby populations.

facts.text: Dark-eyed juncos usually nest in a cup-shaped hollow on the ground, well hidden by vegetation or other material.
facts.quote: Dark-eyed juncos usually nest in a cup-shaped depression on the ground, well-hidden by vegetation or other material, although nests are sometimes found in the lower branches of a shrub or tree.

facts.text: Junco chicks born at UCLA during the COVID lockdown had bills that more closely resembled those of local wildland birds.
facts.quote: Birds born during the lockdown had bills that more closely resembled local wildland birds.

facts.text: In winter, dark-eyed juncos are the most common birds at feeders in many places.
facts.quote: In winter, dark-eyed juncos are familiar in and around towns, and in many places are the most common birds at feeders.

facts.text: Herring gulls may drum their feet on the ground like Irish stepdancing to bring earthworms up to the surface.
facts.quote: European herring gulls may be observed rhythmically drumming their feet upon the ground for prolonged periods of time in a behaviour that superficially resembles Irish stepdancing, for the purpose of creating vibrations in the soil, driving earthworms to the surface, which are then consumed by the gull.

facts.text: Herring gulls have been seen using pieces of bread as bait to catch goldfish.
facts.quote: In addition, the European herring gull has been observed using pieces of bread as bait with which to catch goldfish.

facts.text: Despite the name, herring gulls have no special preference for herrings.
facts.quote: Despite their name, they have no special preference for herrings — in fact, examinations have shown that echinoderms and crustaceans comprised a greater portion of these gulls' stomach contents than fish, although fish is the principal element of regurgitations for nestlings.

facts.text: A herring gull has been recorded living to the age of 49 years.
facts.quote: Like most gulls, European herring gulls are long-lived, with a maximum age of 49 years recorded.

facts.text: Some herring gulls may even go shoplifting, stealing food from stores and making off with it.
facts.quote: In some circumstances, these interactions may even lead to the birds engaging in "shoplifting", actively stealing food from stores and making off with it.

facts.text: The Tennessee warbler's scientific name, peregrina, comes from a Latin word meaning "wanderer."
facts.quote: The specific name peregrina is from  Latin  peregrinus "wanderer".

facts.text: Alexander Wilson named this bird after finding one by Tennessee's Cumberland River in 1832, outside the species's usual range.
facts.quote: The bird was named by Alexander Wilson, who discovered an individual by Tennessee's Cumberland River in 1832, although this location is outside of the species's usual range.

facts.text: This warbler's favorite food is the spruce budworm, and its population rises and falls with the amount of budworm.
facts.quote: The Tennessee warbler feeds mainly on insects and prefers the spruce budworm. This species fluctuates in population with the quantity of the budworm.

facts.text: Tennessee warblers nest alone, but after breeding they join mixed flocks.
facts.quote: It is solitary while nesting, but forms mixed flocks after breeding.

facts.text: The female builds a cup-shaped nest of grasses and moss, sometimes above a bog, and lays 4–7 white eggs with brown splotches.
facts.quote: It makes a cup-shaped nest of dried grasses and moss lined with finer grasses, stems and hair. The nest can be placed on the ground or above a bog in moss or in the base of a shrub. The nest is built by the female, and she lays 4–7 white eggs with brown splotches on them.

facts.text: A female gadwall's call is like a female mallard's quack but higher-pitched, written as gag-ag-ag-ag.
facts.quote: Females give a call similar to the quack of a female mallard but higher-pitched, transcribed as gag-ag-ag-ag.

facts.text: Gadwalls dive for food better than other dabbling ducks, and may steal food from diving birds such as coots.
facts.quote: They can also dive underwater for food, more proficiently than other dabbling ducks, and may also steal food from diving birds such as coots.

facts.text: A gadwall subspecies, Coues's gadwall, once lived only on Teraina, a Pacific coral atoll, and went extinct around 1874.
facts.quote: †M. s. couesi (formerly A. s. couesi), Coues's gadwall, extinct c. 1874, was formerly found only on Teraina, a coral atoll in the Pacific Ocean.

facts.text: Gadwalls nest on the ground, often some distance from water.
facts.quote: It nests on the ground, often some distance from water.

facts.text: In one courtship display, a male gadwall sends a stream of water droplets toward a nearby female.
facts.quote: The grunt-whistle is similar to that of mallards, where the male rears his outstretched head with the bill dipped into water, displacing a stream of water droplets towards a nearby female as the bill is raised against the chest.

facts.text: A group of belted kingfishers is called a rattle, a concentration, or a kerfuffle, because they often give a rattling call in flight.
facts.quote: As the kingfisher flies about its habitat, it frequently emits a characteristic rattling call. Accordingly, a small group of belted kingfishers is known as a rattle, concentration, or kerfuffle.

facts.text: Belted kingfishers pound their prey against a perch or the ground to stun and kill it before eating it.
facts.quote: The belted kingfisher has been observed to pound its prey against its perch or the ground to stun and kill it before consumption.

facts.text: Belted kingfisher nest tunnels often slope uphill, which may give chicks an air pocket to survive in if the nest floods.
facts.quote: The nest of the belted kingfisher is a long tunnel and often slopes uphill. One possible reason for the uphill slope is that in case of flooding, the chicks can survive in the air pocket formed by the elevated end of the tunnel.

facts.text: Both belted kingfisher parents dig the nest tunnel in a river bank or sand bank.
facts.quote: This bird nests in a horizontal tunnel made in a river bank or sand bank and excavated by both parents.

facts.text: Students want the belted kingfisher to be the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign mascot, partly because females are orange and blue.
facts.quote: There is a campaign to make the belted kingfisher the official mascot of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Students and alumni in support of the proposed mascot have noted that female belted kingfishers are orange and blue, which corresponds to the University’s colors.

facts.text: Red-bellied woodpeckers drum on aluminum roofs, metal gutters and transformer boxes in cities to communicate with potential mates.
facts.quote: They tap on hollow trees, and even on aluminum roofs, metal guttering and transformer boxes in urban environments, to communicate with potential partners.

facts.text: In the U.S. Midwest, a red-bellied woodpecker can remove up to 85 percent of emerald ash borer larvae in a single infested ash tree.
facts.quote: It is a major predator of the invasive emerald ash borer in the U.S. Midwest, removing up to 85 percent of borer larvae in a single infested ash tree.

facts.text: Red-bellied woodpeckers hide berries and acorns deep in natural crevices to keep them away from competing species.
facts.quote: Field observations indicate that woodpeckers partake extensively in food storage, hiding items such as berries and acorns deep within natural crevices to protect them from interspecific competitors.

facts.text: Squirrels and bats use the cavities that red-bellied woodpeckers excavate as shelter.
facts.quote: By excavating cavities, they play an important role in forest communities for other species as well. For example, squirrels and bats use these cavities as shelter.

facts.text: The male picks a nest hole, then seeks his mate's approval through mutual tapping.
facts.quote: The male red-bellied woodpecker takes the initiative in locating a nest hole. He will then seek approval from his mate by mutual tapping.

facts.text: Red-headed woodpeckers have been known to stuff food in tree cavities, crevices, and under tree bark.
facts.quote: They have been known to stuff food in tree cavities, crevices, and under tree bark.

facts.text: Red-headed woodpeckers eat insects, nuts and fruit, and sometimes small rodents or even the eggs of other birds.
facts.quote: The red-headed woodpecker is omnivorous, eating insects, seeds, fruits, berries, nuts, and occasionally small rodents―even the eggs of other birds.

facts.text: A female red-headed woodpecker picks the nest site and shows her choice by tapping on it.
facts.quote: Females choose the location of their new nesting cavity, indicating their choice by tapping on a site.

facts.text: If a fledgling is still in the territory after a few weeks, the parents chase it out to force it to disperse.
facts.quote: Most of the fledglings will disperse on their own within a couple of weeks, but if a fledgling is still in the territory after a few weeks the parents will chase them out to force them to disperse.

facts.text: In 1996, the U.S. Postal Service issued a 2-cent stamp showing a perched red-headed woodpecker.
facts.quote: In 1996, the United States Postal Service issued a 2-cent postage stamp depicting a perched red-headed woodpecker.

facts.text: A wild turkey's gobble can be heard up to a mile away.
facts.quote: The gobble of a wild turkey can be heard up to a mile away.

facts.text: Male turkeys sometimes attack parked cars and reflective surfaces, thinking they see another turkey in their territory.
facts.quote: Male toms occasionally will attack parked cars and reflective surfaces, thinking they see another turkey and must defend their territory.

facts.text: Benjamin Franklin never publicly suggested the turkey as a national symbol; the story has been called a myth.
facts.quote: Franklin never publicly voiced opposition to the bald eagle as a national symbol, nor did he ever publicly suggest the turkey as a national symbol. The story has been called a myth.

facts.text: Turkeys sometimes forage with deer and squirrels, and by doing so each helps the others watch for predators.
facts.quote: Turkeys will occasionally forage with deer and squirrels, and may even play with them. By foraging together, each can help the other watch for predators with their different senses: the deer with their improved olfactory sense, the turkey with its superior sight, and squirrels providing an additional set of eyes from the air.

facts.text: Pilgrims brought turkeys from England to Massachusetts, unaware that a larger close relative already lived in the forests there.
facts.quote: By 1620 it was common enough so that Pilgrim settlers of Massachusetts could bring turkeys with them from England, unaware that it had a larger close relative already occupying the forests of Massachusetts.

facts.text: Female swamp sparrows give a series of chips as they leave the nest, probably to ward off attacks by their mate or neighboring males.
facts.quote: Females give a series of chips as they leave the nest, probably to ward off attacks by their mate or neighboring males.

facts.text: In winter swamp sparrows eat mostly fruit and seeds, but in breeding season they switch to mainly arthropods.
facts.quote: In winter, their diet is principally fruit and seeds, while during the breeding season their diet is mainly arthropods.

facts.text: A male swamp sparrow can have a repertoire of several different trills.
facts.quote: A male can have a repertoire of several different trills.

facts.text: The southern edge of the swamp sparrow's breeding range largely lines up with the Line of Maximum Glaciation.
facts.quote: The southern edge of their breeding range coincides largely with the Line of Maximum Glaciation.

facts.text: Mockingbirds can remember an individual human who earlier approached and threatened their nest.
facts.quote: In a paper published in 2009, researchers found that mockingbirds were able to recall an individual human who, earlier in the study, had approached and threatened the mockingbirds' nest.

facts.text: Mockingbirds imitate cats, dogs, frogs, crickets, and even car alarms.
facts.quote: It imitates not only birds, but also other animals such as cats, dogs, frogs, and crickets and sounds from artificial items such as unoiled wheels and even car alarms.

facts.text: A mockingbird incident involving a postal carrier in Tulsa, Oklahoma led to a warning letter being sent to residents.
facts.quote: One incident in Tulsa, Oklahoma involving a postal carrier resulted in the distribution of a warning letter to residents.

facts.text: Thomas Jefferson had several pet mockingbirds, including one named Dick.
facts.quote: Thomas Jefferson had several pet mockingbirds, including a bird named "Dick".

facts.text: Mockingbird imitations may convince humans, but they often fail to fool other birds, such as the Florida scrub jay.
facts.quote: As convincing as these imitations may be to humans, they often fail to fool other birds, such as the Florida scrub jay.

facts.text: Cowbird eggs have turned up in nests of at least 220 host species, including hummingbirds and raptors.
facts.quote: The brown-headed cowbird eggs have been documented in nests of at least 220 host species, including hummingbirds and raptors.

facts.text: Before European settlement, brown-headed cowbirds followed bison herds across the prairies.
facts.quote: Before European settlement,  brown-headed cowbirds followed bison herds across the prairies.

facts.text: Young cowbirds recognize a species "password" in the calls of other cowbirds, which helps them find and join their own flock.
facts.quote: Cowbird brains are wired to respond to the vocalizations of other cowbirds, allowing young to find and join flocks of their own species. These vocalizations are consistent across all cowbird populations, and serve as a sort of species-recognition password.

facts.text: American yellow warblers deal with a cowbird egg by burying it under nest material, while brown thrashers toss it out of the nest.
facts.quote: Others, like the American yellow warbler, bury the foreign egg under nest material, where it perishes. The brown thrasher physically ejects the egg from the nest.

facts.text: Despite its name, flies make up only a small share of this flycatcher's diet; it prefers butterflies, moths, beetles and wasps.
facts.quote: Despite the "flycatcher" of the bird's name, flies, along with spiders, make up only a small percentage of its diet; it prefers prey such as butterflies, moths, beetles, grasshoppers, crickets, and bees and wasps.

facts.text: Its nests can include bits of shed snakeskin, animal fur and feathers, and even string, tape, cloth and plastic.
facts.quote: The nest itself is built within 2 to 4 days and is composed mostly of vegetation and plant fibers, such as grasses, moss, leaves, but also pieces of animal fur and feathers, pieces of shed snakeskin, and artificial materials (ex: strings, tape, cloth, and plastic objects).

facts.text: When it eats berries, it swallows them whole and later regurgitates the pits.
facts.quote: Fruits and berries, when consumed are swallowed whole and the pits later regurgitated.

facts.text: It sometimes brakes and hovers to pick insects off leaves, and sometimes it crashes into the foliage while doing it.
facts.quote: They can also be seen abruptly braking and hovering, picking insects or small fruits off of leaves, trunks or other surfaces, sometimes crashing into the foliage in the process.

facts.text: When Linnaeus described this bird in 1758, he placed it with the thrushes.
facts.quote: The great crested flycatcher was formally described in 1758 by the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus in the tenth edition of his Systema Naturae. He placed it with the thrushes in the genus Turdus and coined the binomial name Turdus crinitus.

facts.text: Night herons toss buoyant objects onto the water to lure fish, a rare example of tool use among birds.
facts.quote: They are among the seven heron species observed to engage in bait fishing; luring or distracting fish by tossing edible or inedible buoyant objects into water within their striking range – a rare example of tool use among birds.

facts.text: During courtship, a night heron's legs turn bright salmon-pink and the bare skin around its eyes turns blue.
facts.quote: For a short period during courtship at the start of the nesting season, the legs of adults turn bright salmon-pink, and the bare skin around the eyes blue.

facts.text: A colony of night herons has regularly summered at the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., for more than a century.
facts.quote: A colony of the herons has regularly summered at the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., for more than a century.

facts.text: Oakland named the night heron its official city bird, partly because the birds held up against efforts to displace them.
facts.quote: Their ever presence at Oakland's Lake Merritt and throughout the city's downtown area, as well as their resilience to the urban environment and displacement efforts, have led to them being named Oakland's official city bird.

facts.text: Its scientific name, Nycticorax, combines the Ancient Greek words for "night" and "raven".
facts.quote: The epithet nycticorax is from Ancient Greek and combines nux, nuktos meaning "night" and korax meaning "raven".

facts.text: Ospreys and owls are the only raptors with reversible outer toes, which helps them grip slippery fish.
facts.quote: The osprey and owls are the only raptors whose outer toes are reversible, allowing them to grasp their prey with two toes in front and two behind. This is particularly helpful when they grab slippery fish.

facts.text: As an osprey dives, it adjusts its flight angle to account for the way refraction distorts the fish's image.
facts.quote: As an osprey dives, it adjusts the angle of its flight to account for the distortion of the fish's image caused by refraction.

facts.text: Large osprey nests on utility poles can weigh about 135 kg and have caused power outages.
facts.quote: As wide as 2 m and weighing about 135 kg (298 lb), large nests on utility poles may be fire hazards and have caused power outages.

facts.text: The oldest European wild osprey on record lived to be 26 years and 11 months old.
facts.quote: The oldest European wild osprey on record lived to be 26 years and 11 months of age.

facts.text: A medieval belief held that fish were so mesmerized by the osprey that they turned belly-up in surrender.
facts.quote: A medieval belief held that fish were so mesmerised by the osprey that they turned belly-up in surrender, and this is referenced by Shakespeare in Act 4 Scene 5 of Coriolanus:

facts.text: House sparrows have been recorded breeding in an English coal mine 640 m (2,100 ft) below ground.
facts.quote: It has been recorded breeding in an English coal mine 640 m (2,100 ft) below ground, and feeding on the Empire State Building's observation deck at night.

facts.text: House sparrows can work out how to open automatic doors to get into supermarkets.
facts.quote: It can perform complex tasks to obtain food, such as opening automatic doors to enter supermarkets, clinging to hotel walls to watch vacationers on their balconies, and nectar robbing kowhai flowers.

facts.text: House sparrows reached the Falkland Islands as stowaways on whaling ships.
facts.quote: The house sparrow is also established in the Falkland Islands, where it arrived as a stowaway on whaling ships.

facts.text: At feeding stations and nests, female house sparrows are dominant despite their smaller size.
facts.quote: At feeding stations and nests, female house sparrows are dominant despite their smaller size, and they can fight over males in the breeding season.

facts.text: Birds from England were released in New York City in 1852 to control the linden moth.
facts.quote: The first of many successful introductions to North America occurred when birds from England were released in New York City, in 1852, intended to control the ravages of the linden moth.

facts.text: A blue grosbeak caught in Ohio in 2017 was confirmed to be 10 years old, beating the earlier known record of seven years.
facts.quote: A blue grosbeak captured in Ohio in 2017 was confirmed to be 10 years old, surpassing the previously known record for the species at seven years.

facts.text: Blue grosbeaks have spread northward over the past century or two, likely helped by humans clearing forests.
facts.quote: The range of this species has expanded northward over the past century or two, likely aided by the clearing of forests by humans.

facts.text: Blue grosbeaks mostly eat insects, but they will also eat snails, spiders, seeds, grains, and wild fruits.
facts.quote: It eats mostly insects, but it will also eat snails, spiders, seeds, grains, and wild fruits.

facts.text: A few blue grosbeaks winter as far south as northern South America, and the southernmost record is from eastern Ecuador.
facts.quote: They are uncommon within their range, migrating south to Central America and in very small numbers to northern South America; the southernmost record comes from eastern Ecuador.

facts.text: Indigo buntings often migrate at night and use the stars to navigate.
facts.quote: The indigo bunting often migrates during the night, using the stars to navigate.

facts.text: The female builds a nest of leaves, grasses and bark, lined with soft grass or deer hair and bound with spider web.
facts.quote: The nest itself is constructed of leaves, coarse grasses, stems, and strips of bark, lined with soft grass or deer hair and is bound with spider web. It is constructed by the female, who cares for the eggs alone.

facts.text: The male may feed newly fledged young while the female sits on the next clutch of eggs.
facts.quote: Most pairs raise two broods per year, and the male may feed newly fledged young while the females incubate the next clutch of eggs.

facts.text: Each male has one complex song, which he sings from perches like posts, wires and bush-tops.
facts.quote: Each male has a single complex song, which he sings while perched on elevated objects, such as posts, wires, and bush-tops.

facts.text: An indigo bunting abandons its nest if a cowbird egg appears before it lays its own, but accepts the egg after that.
facts.quote: Indigo buntings abandon their nest if a cowbird egg appears before they lay any of their own eggs, but accept the egg after that point.

facts.text: When a cliff swallow finds a good feeding spot, it gives a special squeak call, and large groups of colony neighbors arrive.
facts.quote: The "squeak" call is of great interest to researchers because this is the special vocalisation made at a distance from the colony when a bird encounters a good foraging area. When this call is heard, large groups of their colony "neighbours" will arrive at the location.

facts.text: Cliff swallows have been seen skipping one to five years between breeding at the same place to avoid parasites.
facts.quote: The cliff swallows have been observed to skip from one to five years between breeding at the same place to avoid parasite infestations, but some pairs will return annually to the same site.

facts.text: At dusk, cliff swallows often fly overhead in a tightly coordinated flock that may look like one large organism.
facts.quote: When the swallows return to the nesting site at dusk, they often fly in a tightly coordinated flock overhead, in such close synchronization that they may appear as one large organism.

facts.text: Young cliff swallows are said to have a unique call by about 15 days old, so parents can pick their chick out in the colony.
facts.quote: Juvenile cliff swallows are said to have established a unique call by the approximate age of 15 days, which allows the parents to identify their chick from others in the colony.

facts.text: A 1940 song, 'When the Swallows Come Back to Capistrano,' celebrates the cliff swallows' yearly migration to a California mission.
facts.quote: They nest at the church of Mission San Juan Capistrano, where their annual migration is culturally celebrated. A 1940 song by Leon René, "When the Swallows Come Back to Capistrano", celebrates this event.

facts.text: Pheasants prefer to run, but when startled they burst upward with a whirring wing sound and kok kok kok calls.
facts.quote: While common pheasants are able short-distance fliers, they prefer to run. If startled however, they can suddenly burst upwards at great speed, with a distinctive "whirring" wing sound and often giving kok kok kok calls to alert conspecifics.

facts.text: Pheasant chicks grow fast and are flying after 12–14 days.
facts.quote: After hatching they grow quickly, flying after 12–14 days, resembling adults by only 15 weeks of age.

facts.text: Pheasant eggs hatch faster than many nestmates' eggs, so a host parent may leave her own unhatched eggs behind.
facts.quote: Pheasant eggs also have a shorter incubation time than many of their nestmates, which may result in the individual watching over the nest to abandon her own eggs after the pheasants hatch, thinking that the remaining eggs are not viable.

facts.text: The ring-necked pheasant is South Dakota's state bird, and it's one of only two US state birds not native to the country.
facts.quote: The ring-necked pheasant is the state bird of South Dakota, one of only two US state birds that is not a species native to the United States.

facts.text: In the UK, about 50 million captive-reared pheasants are released each summer.
facts.quote: In the United Kingdom, about 50 million pheasants reared in captivity are released each summer, a number which has significantly increased since the 1980s.

facts.text: Of 70 eastern U.S. migratory songbirds, only male rose-breasted grosbeaks made sperm while still far south of where they breed.
facts.quote: Rose-breasted grosbeaks were the only one of 70 migratory songbird species in the eastern United States shown in males to have produced sperm while still far south of their breeding location.

facts.text: Rose-breasted grosbeaks apparently recognize cowbird eggs and have been seen aggressively chasing cowbirds away from the nest.
facts.quote: Although frequently targeted by the brood parasite, the brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater), the rose-breasted grosbeak is apparently able to recognize cowbird eggs and has been seen to aggressively displace cowbirds near the nest.

facts.text: The rose-breasted grosbeak's song is a sweeter, more refined version of the American robin's.
facts.quote: The song is a subdued mellow warbling, resembling a more refined, sweeter version of the American robin's (Turdus migratorius).

facts.text: Male grosbeaks do roughly a third of the incubating, and incubation can last 11 to 14 days.
facts.quote: Males do a third of the incubation roughly, the female doing the remaining amount, and incubation can last from 11 to 14 days.

facts.text: Grosbeak nestlings start at 5 grams, then after 3–6 days of age they gain at least 3 grams each day.
facts.quote: Nestlings are 5 g (0.18 oz) at hatching and after 3–6 days of age, they gain at least 3 g (0.11 oz) each day.

facts.text: One eastern towhee was recorded as a vagrant in Great Britain in 1966, far from its usual home in eastern North America.
facts.quote: One individual of this species was recorded as a vagrant to western Europe, a single bird in Great Britain in 1966.

facts.text: Towhees scratch for food on the ground by kicking both feet backward at the same time.
facts.quote: When foraging on the ground eastern towhees use a scratching technique where both feet kick back simultaneously.

facts.text: The name "towhee" imitates one of its most common calls, a short, two-part call that rises in pitch.
facts.quote: The name "towhee" is onomatopoeic description of one of the towhee's most common calls, a short, two-part call rising in pitch and sometimes also called a "chewink" call.

facts.text: The towhee's song lasts around one second: a sharp "drink!" followed by a short trill on "teeeeea".
facts.quote: The song is a short drink your teeeeea lasting around one second, starting with a sharp call ("drink!") and ending with a short trill "teeeeea".

facts.text: Even the loggerhead shrike, a bird scarcely larger than a towhee, is among the predators of eastern towhees.
facts.quote: Other predators include barred (Strix varia), short-eared (Asio flammeus) and eastern screech-owls (Megascops asio) and even the loggerhead shrike (Lanius ludovicianus), which is scarcely larger than a towhee.

facts.text: Scarlet tanagers rake bees, wasps and hornets against a branch to remove the stingers before eating them.
facts.quote: While summer tanagers are famous for this feeding method, when capturing bees, wasps, and hornets, scarlet tanagers also rake the prey against a branch  to remove their stingers before consumption.

facts.text: Scarlet tanagers hunt by "sallying": flying out to catch an insect in midair, then returning to the same general perch.
facts.quote: Scarlet tanagers are often out of sight, foraging high in trees, sometimes flying out to catch insects in flight and then returning to the same general perch, in a hunting style known as "sallying".

facts.text: By 10 days old, scarlet tanager nestlings weigh 70% of what their parent weighs.
facts.quote: The average weight at hatching is 3.97 g (0.140 oz), with the nestlings increasing their weight to 20–22 g (0.71–0.78 oz) by 10 days, or 70% of the parent's weight.

facts.text: Scarlet tanagers were classed as tanagers until 2009, when genetic studies moved them into the cardinal family.
facts.quote: It was placed in the tanager family (Thraupidae) until 2009, but was moved to Cardinalidae following several genetic studies indicating the Piranga tanagers are more closely related to cardinals and their allies.

facts.text: The genus name Piranga comes from a Tupi name for an unknown small bird.
facts.quote: The genus name Piranga is from Tupi Tijepiranga, the name for an unknown small bird, and the specific olivacea is from Neo-Latin olivaceus, "olive-green".

facts.text: One chickadee warning call about a pygmy owl contained 23 dees.
facts.quote: In one case, a warning call about a pygmy owl—a prime threat to chickadees—contained 23 dees.

facts.text: A chickadee's hippocampus is believed to grow so it can remember its food cache spots, then shrink as the caches are used up.
facts.quote: While the exact reason for this seasonal change is unknown, it is believed that the hippocampus grows to allow the chickadee to remember its cache locations, and then shrinks as those caches are used up.

facts.text: On cold winter nights, chickadees can drop their body temperature by as much as 12°C to save energy.
facts.quote: On cold winter nights, these birds can reduce their body temperature by as much as 12°C (from their normal temperature of about 42°C) to conserve energy.

facts.text: A nesting female chickadee may hiss like a snake, probably to discourage nest predators.
facts.quote: If an unusual disturbance occurs at the nest entrance, the incubating female may utter an explosive hiss like that of a snake, a probable adaptation to discourage nest predators.

facts.text: Red-breasted nuthatches react more strongly to chickadee alarm calls that signal a higher threat.
facts.quote: Red-breasted nuthatch have even been observed reacting more strongly to higher-threat alarm calls, indicating some understanding of their syntax.

facts.text: To save energy in extremely cold winters, Carolina chickadees deliberately lower their body temperature in a state called torpor.
facts.quote: Carolina chickadees are able to lower their body temperatures to induce an intentional state of hypothermia called torpor. They do this to conserve energy during extremely cold winters.

facts.text: The name "chickadee" is a vocal imitation of the bird's own call.
facts.quote: The origin of this bird name is onomatopoeic, a vocal imitation of its call.

facts.text: Chickadees call out whenever they find good food, which helps other birds in mixed flocks find it more efficiently.
facts.quote: Mixed flocks stay together because the chickadees call out whenever they find a good source of food. This calling out forms cohesion for the group, allowing the other birds to find food more efficiently.

facts.text: The Carolina chickadee sings a four-note see-dee-see-dee, while the black-capped chickadee's song has two or three notes.
facts.quote: The calls and song between the Carolina chickadee and the black-capped chickadee differ subtly to an experienced ear: the Carolina chickadee's chick-a-dee call is faster and higher-pitched than that of the black-capped chickadee, and the Carolina chickadee has a four-note see-dee-see-dee song, whereas the black-capped chickadee has a two- or three-note song.

facts.text: Female Carolina chickadees usually sleep in the nest cavity, while males normally sleep on a nearby branch.
facts.quote: While females usually sleep in the nest cavity, males will normally sleep on a nearby branch.

facts.text: Blue-gray gnatcatchers often build their nests far out on a branch, held together with spider silk and lichen.
facts.quote: Their nests are often built far out on a tree's branch with spider silks and lichen plants holding them together.

facts.text: Blue-gray gnatcatchers may hover over leaves to snatch prey, or fly out to catch insects in midair.
facts.quote: They may hover over foliage while snatching prey (gleaning), or fly to catch insects in flight (hawking).

facts.text: A blue-gray gnatcatcher often holds its tail upright when it defends its territory or looks for food.
facts.quote: The tail is often held upright while defending territory or searching for food.

facts.text: Male blue-gray gnatcatchers often help build the nest, incubate the eggs, and feed the young.
facts.quote: The males often work to build nests, help incubate and raise the young, as well as feed the children.

facts.text: A blue-gray gnatcatcher can raise up to two broods in one season.
facts.quote: The blue-gray gnatcatcher can raise up to two broods in a season.

facts.text: Purple martin roosts can be so big that when the birds take off to forage, Doppler weather radar picks them up as rings.
facts.quote: These flocks can be so large that when they take off from these roosts to forage, the activity is detected on Doppler weather radar as rings.

facts.text: Approaching their nest site, purple martins dive at great speed with wings tucked, just like a hunting peregrine falcon.
facts.quote: When approaching their nesting site, they will dive from the sky at great speeds with their wings tucked, just like the peregrine falcon does when hunting smaller birds.

facts.text: Despite popular belief, mosquitoes are not a large part of a purple martin's diet, because the birds usually fly relatively high.
facts.quote: They usually fly relatively high, so, contrary to popular opinion, mosquitoes do not form a large part of their diet.

facts.text: Cherokee hung hollow gourds so martins would nest and feed their young thousands of insects that would otherwise eat crops.
facts.quote: The human-avian relationship was in place even before the population crash in the 20th century; Cherokee were known to have hollowed out gourds and hung them on wooden snags and posts in the pre-colonial era. They erected them so that the adult birds would build nests and then feed thousands of insects to their young each day that would otherwise be eating their crops.

facts.text: The martin's species name, subis, is Latin for a bird a Roman author said could break eagles' eggs.
facts.quote: The specific epithet subis is Latin for a bird mentioned by the Roman author Nigidius Figulus that could break eagles' eggs.

facts.text: A group of grackles is called a "plague."
facts.quote: When grackles are in a group, they are referred to as a "plague".

facts.text: A keel in a grackle's bill lets it crack and cut hard nuts or kernels.
facts.quote: Grackles have a unique adaptation in the keel within their bill which allows them to crack and cut hard nuts or kernels.

facts.text: Common grackles rub insects on their feathers, called "anting," possibly to apply liquids such as formic acid.
facts.quote: Along with some other species of grackles, the common grackle is known to practice "anting", rubbing insects on its feathers possibly to apply liquids such as formic acid secreted by the insects.

facts.text: Grackles often snatch food right out of another bird's beak.
facts.quote: Grackles at outdoor eating areas often wait eagerly until someone drops some food. They rush forward and try to grab it, often snatching food out of the beak of another bird.

facts.text: A grackle's song can occasionally sound like a power line buzzing.
facts.quote: It also occasionally sounds like a power line buzzing.

facts.text: Golden-crowned kinglets may form tight huddles to get through the winter.
facts.quote: Golden-crowned kinglets may form tight huddles when overwintering.

facts.text: The golden-crowned kinglet builds a well-hidden hanging cup nest suspended from a conifer branch.
facts.quote: Its nest is a well-concealed hanging cup suspended from a conifer branch.

facts.text: Golden-crowned kinglets eat insects, especially caterpillars, along with insect eggs and spiders.
facts.quote: The golden-crowned kinglet is insectivorous, foraging in trees or shrubs, where it eats insects (especially caterpillars), insect eggs and spiders.

facts.text: The kinglet's name comes from a Latin word meaning "a king," a nod to the crests on adult kinglets.
facts.quote: The names of the family, Regulidae, and the genus, Regulus, are derived from the Latin regulus, a diminutive of rex, "a king", and refer to the characteristic orange or yellow crests of adult kinglets.

facts.text: Golden-crowned kinglets tend not to fear people who walk up to them.
facts.quote: It produces a series of high-pitched calls on a single note, and tends not to fear human approach.

facts.text: In northern Ohio, bank swallows now arrive in numbers about 10 days earlier than they did 100 years ago.
facts.quote: In northern Ohio, they arrive in numbers by mid-April, about 10 days earlier than they did 100 years ago.

facts.text: Bank swallows nest together in colonies of anywhere from a dozen to many hundred pairs, depending on available space.
facts.quote: The sand martin is sociable in its nesting habits; from a dozen to many hundred pairs will nest close together, according to available space.

facts.text: A bank swallow nest sits in a chamber at the end of a burrow bored in sand or gravel, and it soon becomes a hotbed of parasites.
facts.quote: The nests are at the end of tunnels ranging from a few inches to three or four feet in length, bored in sand or gravel. The actual nest is a litter of straw and feathers in a chamber at the end of the burrow; it soon becomes a hotbed of parasites.

facts.text: When a falcon or crow passes by, bank swallows give a harsh alarm call so they can team up to drive the predator away.
facts.quote: The harsh alarm is heard when a passing falcon, crow or other suspected predator requires combined action to drive it away.

facts.text: Early in spring, bank swallows flit over big bodies of water, searching for early flies, before they visit their nesting sites.
facts.quote: At first, they flit over the larger bodies of water alone, in search of early flies.

facts.text: Eastern phoebes often build their nests on human structures such as bridges and buildings.
facts.quote: The eastern phoebe often nests on human structures such as bridges and buildings.

facts.text: A phoebe nest is an open cup with a mud base, lined with moss and grass.
facts.quote: The nest is an open cup with a mud base and lined with moss and grass, built in a crevice in a rock or man-made site; two to six eggs are laid.

facts.text: Eastern phoebes pump their tails up and down when perched on a branch, like other phoebes do.
facts.quote: it pumps its tail up and down like other phoebes when perching on a branch.

facts.text: The eastern phoebe's song, fee-bee, may be where the bird got its name.
facts.quote: The eastern phoebe's call is a sharp chip, and the song, from which it may get its name, is fee-bee.

facts.text: Robert Frost wrote a 1923 poem about phoebes nesting in a barn on a farm abandoned after the farmhouse burned down.
facts.quote: Phoebes appear in the poem "The Need of Being Versed in Country Things", published in 1923 by Robert Frost. The poem describes phoebes nesting inside a barn on a farm abandoned after the farmhouse burned to the ground.

facts.text: The ovenbird is named for its nest, a domed ground structure woven from vegetation with a side entrance, called the "oven."
facts.quote: The nest, referred to as the "oven" (which gives the bird its name), is a domed structure placed on the ground, woven from vegetation, and containing a side entrance.

facts.text: Chipmunks have been known to burrow right into an ovenbird's nest to eat the young birds.
facts.quote: Chipmunks have been known to burrow directly into the nest to eat the young birds.

facts.text: A female ovenbird can act like an injured bird to distract a predator that comes near her nest.
facts.quote: The female can perform a distraction display, simulating an injured bird, when a potential predator is in the vicinity of the nest.

facts.text: At twilight, male ovenbirds sing a sputtering song with mimicry in the air as they dive back to earth.
facts.quote: Male ovenbirds also utter a sweet chattering song in the air at twilight, after the manner of the skylark, incorporating portions of the main song into a jumble of sputtering notes and mimicry as they dive back to earth.

facts.text: Despite its name, the ovenbird isn't in the ovenbird family of birds.
facts.quote: Despite its name, it is not in the ovenbird family of birds.

facts.text: The bay-breasted warbler's genus name, Setophaga, combines Greek words for "moth" and "-eating."
facts.quote: The genus name Setophaga combines the Ancient Greek σης/sēs, σητος/sētos meaning "moth" with -φαγος/-phagos meaning "-eating".

facts.text: Because fall bay-breasted and blackpoll warblers look so alike, the two are sometimes collectively called "baypoll warblers."
facts.quote: Due to this similarity, the two birds sometimes are collectively called "baypoll warblers".

facts.text: In tropical winter flocks, the bay-breasted warbler is often an aggressive member that bullies smaller species away from food.
facts.quote: These flocks seek food in the forest canopy, and the bay-breasted warbler is often an aggressive member of the unit, bullying smaller species from potential food sources.

facts.text: Bay-breasted warblers often use spider silk in their cup-shaped nests.
facts.quote: The nest is cup-shaped and primarily composed of plant material, with spider silk often utilized as well.

facts.text: Many bay-breasted warblers cross the Gulf of Mexico on their long migration, though some travel along the Mexican shore.
facts.quote: Many individuals cross the Gulf of Mexico on their long-distance migration, although some travel north and south along the Mexican shore.

facts.text: Birdwatchers nickname the yellow-rumped warbler "butter butt" because of its conspicuous yellow rump patch.
facts.quote: the latter giving rise to the species's nickname "butter butt" among birdwatchers

facts.text: The myrtle warbler is the only warbler able to digest waxy wax-myrtle berries, which gave it its name.
facts.quote: When bugs are scarce, the myrtle warbler also eats fruit, including the wax-myrtle berries which gave the myrtle subspecies its name. It is the only warbler able to digest such waxy material.

facts.text: Yellow-rumped warblers have been spotted picking insects off beach seaweed, out of spiderwebs, and even off piles of manure.
facts.quote: Other places yellow-rumped warblers have been spotted foraging include picking at insects on washed-up seaweed at the beach, skimming insects from the surface of rivers and the ocean, picking them out of spiderwebs, and grabbing them off piles of manure.

facts.text: A female lines her nest with fine hair and feathers, sometimes woven so they curl up and over the eggs.
facts.quote: She lines this cup with fine hair and feathers, sometimes woven into the nest in such a way that they curl up and over the eggs.

facts.text: In spring migration, yellow-rumped warblers often use skylight polarization to find their way at dusk.
facts.quote: The birds tend to migrate at night; and during the yellow-rumped warbler's migration in spring, it often relies on skylight polarization as a way to navigate and orient at dusk.

facts.text: Ornithologist Alexander Wilson found this species in magnolias near Fort Adams, Mississippi.
facts.quote: American ornithologist Alexander Wilson found this species in magnolias near Fort Adams, Mississippi.

facts.text: The genus name Setophaga comes from Ancient Greek words meaning "moth" and "eating".
facts.quote: The genus name Setophaga is from Ancient Greek ses, "moth", and phagos, "eating", and the specific  magnolia refers to the type locality.

facts.text: Male magnolia warblers reach the breeding grounds about two weeks before the females do.
facts.quote: Male magnolia warblers go to their breeding grounds about two weeks before the females arrive.

facts.text: Magnolia warblers have been documented hybridizing with American redstarts on two occasions, in Ohio and in Quebec.
facts.quote: Rare hybrids between the magnolia warbler and the congeneric American redstart (Setophaga ruticilla) have been documented on two occasions, in Ohio, USA, and Quebec, Canada.

facts.text: To keep the nest clean, female magnolia warblers eat their chicks' fecal sacs.
facts.quote: In order to keep the nest clean, females eat the fecal sacs of their newborns; as the chicks grow older, both parents simply remove the sacs from the nest.

facts.text: In fall, blackpolls fly nonstop over open water, averaging 2,500 km, one of the longest overwater songbird flights recorded.
facts.quote: In fall, they fly south to the Greater Antilles and the northeastern coasts of South America in a non-stop long-distance migration over open water, averaging 2,500 km (1,600 mi), one of the longest-distance non-stop overwater flights ever recorded for a migratory songbird.

facts.text: Blackpolls are more often heard than seen, and their song is one of the highest-pitched known.
facts.quote: They are more often heard than seen, though their song is one of the highest-pitched known.

facts.text: Before its big ocean flight, a blackpoll nearly doubles its body mass in staging areas.
facts.quote: To accomplish this flight, the blackpoll warbler nearly doubles its body mass in staging areas and takes advantage of a shift in prevailing wind direction to direct it to its destination.

facts.text: Blackpolls breed nearer to the tundra than any other warbler.
facts.quote: Blackpolls breed nearer to the tundra than any other warbler.

facts.text: Blackpoll chicks leave the nest at just 10 days old, before they can fly well.
facts.quote: The eggs are incubated for around 12 days and the young leave the nest when they are only 10 days old before they can fly well.

facts.text: Some young eastern bluebirds stay around the nest to help raise another brood.
facts.quote: Some young stay around the nest to help raise another brood.

facts.text: A threatened female bluebird with no male around will sing, hoping to attract a protective male back to the territory.
facts.quote: If no male is present, a threatened female will begin to sing, hoping to attract a protective male back to the territory.

facts.text: A 2013 study found that Bermuda's bluebirds likely descend from a very small founder group that arrived in the 1600s.
facts.quote: Using simulations and molecular evidence, a 2013 study found that the Bermuda bluebirds likely descend from very small founder population from a single colonization event during the 1600s.

facts.text: In 1934, Thomas Musselman created the first bluebird trail, setting up rows of bluebird houses along roads.
facts.quote: Conservation efforts are seen as early as 1934 when Thomas Musselman created the first bluebird trail by setting up rows of bluebird houses along roads.

facts.text: In Haudenosaunee tradition, the bluebird's call is believed to ward off Sawiskera, the spirit of winter.
facts.quote: In traditional Haudenosaunee cosmology, the call of the bluebird is believed to ward off the icy power of Sawiskera, also referred to as Flint, the spirit of the winter.

facts.text: Its high-pitched, nasal call has been likened to a tin trumpet.
facts.quote: Its call, which has been likened to a tin trumpet, is high-pitched and nasal.

facts.text: The name "nuthatch" comes from "nuthack," for the bird's habit of wedging nuts into bark cracks and hacking them open.
facts.quote: "Nuthatch" is a linguistic corruption of "nuthack", referring to the bird's habit of wedging nuts into cracks in tree bark and hacking at them until they break open.

facts.text: A pair smears sap around its nest hole, probably to help deter predators.
facts.quote: The pair smears sap around the entrance hole, presumably to help deter predators.

facts.text: It climbs down trees headfirst and can "walk" along the underside of branches.
facts.quote: It goes headfirst when climbing down. It can "walk" on the underside of branches.

facts.text: One red-breasted nuthatch that wandered to Europe successfully spent the winter in eastern England.
facts.quote: It is an extremely rare vagrant to Europe, with two records in the western Palearctic; one bird successfully overwintered in eastern England.

facts.text: One white-breasted nuthatch landed on the RMS Queen Mary six hours' sailing east of New York City in October 1963.
facts.quote: One bird landed on the RMS Queen Mary six hours' sailing east of New York City in October 1963.

facts.text: After leaving its nest hole, it wipes fur or vegetation around the entrance, making the nest harder for predators to sniff out.
facts.quote: When a bird leaves the nest hole, it wipes around the entrance with a piece of fur or vegetation; this makes it more difficult for a predator to find the nest using its sense of smell.

facts.text: It may smear crushed blister beetles around its nest entrance, perhaps to keep squirrels, its chief rivals for tree holes, away.
facts.quote: The nuthatch may also smear blister beetles around the entrance to its nest, and it has been suggested that the unpleasant smell from the crushed insects deters squirrels, its chief competitor for natural tree cavities.

facts.text: It has the unusual habit of removing its feces from the roost site in the morning.
facts.quote: This species of nuthatch roosts in tree holes or behind loose bark when not breeding and has the unusual habit of removing its feces from the roost site in the morning.

facts.text: The average lifespan is estimated at two years, but the record is twelve years and nine months.
facts.quote: The estimated average lifespan of the white-breasted nuthatch is two years, but the record is twelve years and nine months.

facts.text: A shoveler's wide bill has comb-like edges that work like sieves to skim crustaceans and plankton from the water's surface.
facts.quote: Their wide, flat bill is equipped with well-developed lamellae – small, comb-like structures on the edge of the bill that act like sieves, allowing the birds to skim crustaceans and plankton from the surface of the water.

facts.text: Shovelers that winter in the Indian subcontinent fly over the Himalayas, often resting in wetlands just south of the mountains.
facts.quote: Those wintering in the Indian subcontinent make the taxing journey over the Himalayas, often taking a break in wetlands just south of the Himalayas before continuing further south to warmer regions.

facts.text: During courtship, a dozen or more male shovelers can chase a single female.
facts.quote: Drakes also engage in elaborate courtship displays, both on the water and in the air; not uncommonly, a dozen or more males maypursue a single hen.

facts.text: The male shoveler makes a clunking call, while the female quacks much like a mallard.
facts.quote: The male has a clunking call, whereas the female has a mallard-like quack.

facts.text: The shoveler's genus name, Spatula, is Latin for 'spoon' or 'spatula'.
facts.quote: The name Spatula is the Latin for a "spoon" or "spatula".

facts.text: Blue-winged teal ducklings can walk to water within 12 hours of hatching but don't fledge until they are 6 to 7 weeks old.
facts.quote: Blue-winged teal ducklings can walk to water within 12 hours after hatching but do not fledge until 6 to 7 weeks.

facts.text: During incubation, the drake leaves its mate and goes flightless for 3 to 4 weeks in molting cover.
facts.quote: During incubation, the drake leaves its mate and moves to suitable molting cover where it becomes flightless for a period of 3 to 4 weeks.

facts.text: Blue-winged teal are generally the first ducks to head south in the fall and the last to head north in the spring.
facts.quote: Blue-winged teal are generally the first ducks south in the fall and the last ones north in the spring.

facts.text: Some blue-winged teal fly long distances over open ocean during migration.
facts.quote: During migration, some birds may fly long distances over open ocean.

facts.text: Blue-winged teal nests have been found as far as 1 mile from water.
facts.quote: Blue-winged teal generally nest within several hundred yards of open water; however, nests have been found as far as 1.61 km (1 mi) away from water.

facts.text: Male yellow-bellied sapsuckers usually get to the nesting grounds about a week before the females.
facts.quote: The male usually arrives on the nesting grounds about one week before the female.

facts.text: Hungry sapsucker chicks beg so loudly they can be heard 100 meters away or more.
facts.quote: The chicks beg for food through vocalizations that can be heard 100 metres (330 ft) away or more, likely stimulating the adults to catch more food.

facts.text: Sapsuckers drum on dead trees, not the trees they use for feeding or nesting.
facts.quote: Trees chosen to drum on are dead, and thus are not those used for feeding or nesting.

facts.text: Sapsucker pairs do a courtship dance, bobbing their heads and opening their wings halfway.
facts.quote: Members of a pair also perform a dance where they bob their heads and repeatedly opening their wings halfway.

facts.text: A yellow-bellied sapsucker has very rarely turned up in Ireland and Great Britain, far from its usual range.
facts.quote: This species has occurred as a very rare vagrant to Ireland and Great Britain.

facts.text: A pine siskin can store up to 10% of its body weight in seeds in its crop overnight, giving it extra food on cold days.
facts.quote: In a part of their esophagus called the crop, the species can store up to 10% of their body weight in seeds overnight, providing extra food on cold days.

facts.text: When it gets bitterly cold, pine siskins can rev up their metabolic rate to up to five times normal for several hours.
facts.quote: When temperatures plunge as low as −70 °C (−94 °F), they can accelerate that rate up to five times normal for several hours.

facts.text: Some pine siskin flocks are big enough that 20-30 birds line up to eat from the same feeder.
facts.quote: Indeed some flocks can be large, with 20-30 birds lining up to eat from the same feeder.

facts.text: Mineral deposits can lure pine siskins to winter roads that have been salted to melt snow and ice.
facts.quote: Mineral deposits can lure them to otherwise unattractive habitats like winter road beds that are salted to melt snow and ice.

facts.text: Female pine siskins may never stop incubating their eggs and hatchlings while the male feeds them.
facts.quote: Nests are often heavily insulated with thick plant materials and females may never cease incubating their eggs and hatchlings, while being fed by their male mate.

facts.text: A goldfinch nest is woven so tightly it can hold water, so nestlings can drown in a rainstorm if the parents don't cover it.
facts.quote: The nest is so tightly woven that it can hold water, and it is possible for nestlings to drown following a rainstorm if the parents do not cover the nest.

facts.text: Goldfinches start breeding later in the year than any other finch, possibly because late-summer seeds are so plentiful.
facts.quote: The breeding season begins later in the year than for any other finch and later than any other native North American bird, besides occasionally the sedge wren. This may be related to the abundance of seeds in the late summer months, as seeds represent most of their diet.

facts.text: One of the goldfinch's calls sounds like "po-ta-to-chip" to a listener.
facts.quote: They communicate with several distinct vocalizations, including one that sounds like "po-ta-to-chip" to the listener.

facts.text: In flight, goldfinches often call while flapping and go silent while gliding along their wave-shaped path.
facts.quote: Birds often vocalize during the flapping phase of the pattern and then go silent during the coasting phase.

facts.text: The Cornell Lab of Ornithology calls the goldfinch one of the strictest vegetarians in the bird world.
facts.quote: According to the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, the species is one of the strictest vegetarians in the bird world.

facts.text: A male dickcissel may have up to six mates, but several males fail to attract any at all.
facts.quote: Males may have up to six mates, with most attracting only one or two, and several failing to attract any mates at all.

facts.text: From an open perch, a dickcissel sings a sharp "dick dick" followed by a buzzed "cissel."
facts.quote: From an open perch in a field, this bird's song is a sharp dick dick followed by a buzzed cissel, also transcribed as skee-dlees chis chis chis or dick dick ciss ciss ciss.

facts.text: Dickcissels spread east from the prairies in the early 1800s, but later disappeared as regular breeders along the East Coast.
facts.quote: In the early 1800s, the species spread eastward from the tallgrass prairies, but after 1850, its range decreased, and it eventually disappeared as a regular breeding bird along the East Coast.

facts.text: Some farmers consider dickcissels pests because flocks can eat large quantities of cultivated grains.
facts.quote: They are considered a pest by farmers in some regions because flocks can consume large quantities of cultivated grains.

facts.text: One odd dickcissel was shot with pure white feathers on its face and underside, where the species normally has yellow and buff.
facts.quote: The specimen has foxed today, giving it an altogether beige hue, but when originally shot, the olive areas of the head were grey as the cheeks, and the yellow and buff on face and underside was pure white.

facts.text: Before house sparrows were introduced to North America, chipping sparrows filled much the same niche, living in cities in large numbers.
facts.quote: This bird filled much the same niche as house sparrows now do before their introduction to North America, inhabiting cities in large numbers, and they continue to be associated with human habitations and relatively unafraid of people in areas where house sparrows are not present.

facts.text: A female chipping sparrow builds her nest in about four days, using grass, rootlets, plant fiber and animal hair.
facts.quote: The nest itself is constructed by the female in about four days. It consists of a loose platform of grass and rootlets and open inner cup of plant fiber and animal hair.

facts.text: Chipping sparrows eat seeds year-round, but in the breeding season most of their diet is insects.
facts.quote: The chipping sparrow feeds on seeds year-round, although insects form most of the diet in the breeding season.

facts.text: Chipping sparrows often get their nests parasitized by brown-headed cowbirds, which usually leads to the nest being abandoned.
facts.quote: The chipping sparrow is often brood parasitized by brown-headed cowbirds, usually resulting in the nest being abandoned.

facts.text: You can hear a chipping sparrow's piercing flight call at night while the bird is migrating.
facts.quote: The song is a trill and the bird has a piercing flight call that can be heard while it is migrating at night.

facts.text: Another name for the American tree sparrow is the winter sparrow.
facts.quote: The American tree sparrow (Spizelloides arborea), also known as the winter sparrow, is a medium-sized New World sparrow.

facts.text: John James Audubon put this bird in the first edition of The Birds of America under the name Canada bunting.
facts.quote: First described in 1810 by Alexander Wilson, it was included by John James Audubon in the first edition of The Birds of America under the name Canada bunting.

facts.text: Breeding pairs don't stay together after the breeding season ends.
facts.quote: Breeding pairs do not stay together after the season.

facts.text: Its song is a sweet, high warble that drops in pitch and turns buzzy near the end.
facts.quote: This bird's song is a sweet high warble descending in pitch and becoming buzzy near the finish.

facts.text: Its scientific name combines Ancient Greek for "scraper wing" with Latin for "saw feather".
facts.quote: The genus name, Stelgidopteryx, is from Ancient Greek and means "scraper wing" and the species name, serripennis, is derived from Latin and means "saw feather".

facts.text: These swallows usually nest in burrows that were built by other species.
facts.quote: These burrows are usually built by other species, and measure anywhere from 20 to 200 cm (7.9 to 78.7 in) in length, although most fall between 30 and 100 cm (11.8 and 39.4 in).

facts.text: To drink, they skim the water's surface with a wing and then drink on the wing.
facts.quote: To drink, they skim the surface of the water with their wing and then drink on their wing.

facts.text: In bad weather, several of these swallows can sometimes be seen sharing one burrow.
facts.quote: Sometimes, in adverse weather conditions, several of these swallows can be seen to share a burrow.

facts.text: The female starts incubating with the first egg, so the eggs hatch at different times.
facts.quote: Because the female starts incubating as soon as the first egg is laid, the eggs hatch asynchronously.

facts.text: A tern ringed at its nest in Sweden was found dead in New Zealand five months later, after an estimated 25,000 km flight.
facts.quote: A bird ringed at the nest in Sweden was found dead on Stewart Island, New Zealand, five months later, having flown an estimated 25,000 km (15,000 mi).

facts.text: Early in nesting season, a colony may silently fly low and fast out to sea for no known reason, a behavior called a "dread."
facts.quote: Especially in the early part of the breeding season, for no known reason, most or all of the terns will fly in silence low and fast out to sea. This phenomenon is called a "dread".

facts.text: Common terns can tell individual humans apart and attack familiar people more intensely than strangers.
facts.quote: Adults can discriminate between individual humans, attacking familiar people more intensely than strangers.

facts.text: Common terns can find and dig up their own buried eggs, even with the nest material removed and the sand smoothed over.
facts.quote: Studies show that terns can find and excavate their eggs when they are buried, even if the nest material is removed and the sand smoothed over.

facts.text: One common tern was recorded taking over a spotted sandpiper's nest and laying its eggs alongside the wader's.
facts.quote: There is a record of a common tern taking over a spotted sandpiper nest and laying its eggs with those of the wader.

facts.text: A common way to remember the barred owl's call is the phrase "Who cooks for you, who cooks for you all."
facts.quote: The most common mnemonic device for remembering the call is "Who cooks for you, who cooks for you all."

facts.text: Barred owls plunge into snow to catch voles in hidden winter tunnels, a method once thought peculiar to great grey owls.
facts.quote: Cases of snow-plunging have been verified for barred owls, allowing them to capture prey including voles in subnivean zones that they use as hidden snow tunnels during winter, a hunting method once thought peculiar to great grey owls.

facts.text: A wandering barred owl was once seen flying over Lake Michigan, 30 miles from the nearest land.
facts.quote: A wandering barred owl was once seen flying over Lake Michigan 48 km (30 mi) from the nearest land.

facts.text: Soft, comb-shaped wing feathers make the barred owl's flight functionally silent when it hunts.
facts.quote: As is the case in most owls, the various wing feathers of barred owls are uncharacteristically soft and bear a comb-like shape, which in turn renders their flight functionally silent during their hunts.

facts.text: Eastern meadowlarks build ground nests in depressions such as cattle hoofprints.
facts.quote: Nests are placed on the ground in depressions 1 to 3 inches deep, such as in the hoofprints of cattle, in pastures, meadows, hay fields, and on the edges of marshes.

facts.text: An eastern meadowlark's ground nest is covered with a roof woven from grasses.
facts.quote: The nest is also on the ground, covered with a roof woven from grasses.

facts.text: Eastern meadowlarks sing pure, melancholy whistles, simpler than the jumbled, flutey song of the western meadowlark.
facts.quote: The song of this bird is of pure, melancholy whistles, and thus simpler than the jumbled and flutey song of the western meadowlark; their ranges overlap across central North America.

facts.text: About three-quarters of an eastern meadowlark's diet comes from animal sources like beetles, grasshoppers, and crickets.
facts.quote: About three-quarters of the eastern meadowlark's diet is from animal sources like beetles, grasshoppers, and crickets.

facts.text: Linnaeus confusingly gave this bird's habitat as "America, Africa" when he described it.
facts.quote: Confusingly, Linnaeus specified the habitat as "America, Africa".

facts.text: A wild starling has been seen copying a sound it had heard only once.
facts.quote: In some instances, a wild starling has been observed to mimic a sound it has heard only once.

facts.text: Male starlings often decorate their nests with flowers and fresh greenery, and the female takes it apart once she accepts him as a mate.
facts.quote: Unpaired males find a suitable cavity and begin to build nests in order to attract single females, often decorating the nest with ornaments such as flowers and fresh green material, which the female later disassembles upon accepting him as a mate.

facts.text: Starlings probe soil by opening their bills to widen holes, and they use the same behavior to make holes in plastic garbage bags.
facts.quote: "Probing" involves the bird plunging its beak into the ground randomly and repetitively until an insect has been found, and is often accompanied by bill gaping where the bird opens its beak in the soil to enlarge a hole. This behaviour, first described by Konrad Lorenz and given the German term zirkeln, is also used to create and widen holes in plastic garbage bags.

facts.text: Starling swarms make shapes against the sky that are locally called sort sol, which means "black sun."
facts.quote: Their swarm behaviour creates complex shapes silhouetted against the sky, a phenomenon known locally as sort sol ("black sun").

facts.text: The average starling lives about 2–3 years, but the longevity record is 22 years 11 months.
facts.quote: The average life span is about 2–3 years, with a longevity record of 22 years 11 months.

facts.text: Tree swallow chicks hatch a little apart, which lets the mother choose which chicks to feed when food runs short.
facts.quote: The chicks hatch slightly asynchronously, allowing the female to prioritize which chicks to feed in times of food shortage.

facts.text: Near acidified lakes, tree swallows must fly farther to find calcium for their chicks, like fish bones and clam shells.
facts.quote: In nests near lakes acidified by humans, calcium supplements, primarily fish bones, crayfish exoskeletons, clam shells, and the shells of bird eggs, are harder to find. This forces the adult tree swallow to travel further than usual—sometimes up to 650 m (2,130 ft) away from the nest—to get these calcium supplements.

facts.text: Tree swallow nests of grass and moss are lined with feathers that the males gather, mostly in fights.
facts.quote: The nest cup itself is made from grass, moss, pine needles, and aquatic plants collected mostly by the female, and is lined with feathers gathered primarily by the male in fights.

facts.text: Tree swallows are aggressive in breeding season, but at other times they form flocks sometimes numbering thousands of birds.
facts.quote: Although it is aggressive during the breeding season, this swallow is sociable outside of it, forming flocks sometimes numbering thousands of birds.

facts.text: Nest boxes let tree swallows spread into open habitats; their nesting holes were once found only in forested regions.
facts.quote: The tree swallow nests in structures with pre-existing holes, both natural and artificial. These were once found only in forested regions, but the building of nest boxes has allowed this bird to expand into open habitats.

facts.text: Carolina wrens have nested in tin cans, mailboxes, jacket pockets hanging in sheds, and even a tractor in everyday use.
facts.quote: Nests are located in fragmented or complete cavities in trees, or in man-made structures such as bird-boxes, buildings, tin cans, mailboxes or unorthodox places such as pockets of hanging jackets in sheds or in a tractor in everyday use.

facts.text: In Pennsylvania, Carolina wrens are also called 'mocking wrens' because they occasionally mimic other species.
facts.quote: Occasionally, the wrens mimic other species; in Pennsylvania this trait has caused the bird to be also known as the 'mocking wren'.

facts.text: Male Carolina wrens know at least twenty different song patterns, and thirty two on average.
facts.quote: Males alone sing, and have a repertoire of at least twenty different phrase patterns and on average, thirty two.

facts.text: A Carolina wren can fly straight up from the base of a tree to the top in a single wing-assisted bound.
facts.quote: They are also capable of flying vertically from the base of a tree to the top in a single wing assisted bound.

facts.text: Carolina wrens usually mate for life.
facts.quote: Carolina wrens are both genetically and socially monogamous and will usually mate for life.

facts.text: One thrasher was seen digging a hole, putting an acorn in it, and hitting the acorn until it cracked, which counts as tool use.
facts.quote: In one case, a brown thrasher was observed to dig a hole about 1.5 cm (0.59 in) deep, place an acorn in it and hit the acorn until it cracked, considered to be a form of tool usage.

facts.text: The thrasher's name is believed to come from the thrashing sound it makes digging through ground debris, not from attacking threats.
facts.quote: However, the name does not come from attacking perceived threats, but is believed to have come from the thrashing sound the bird makes when digging through ground debris.

facts.text: A brown thrasher's neck has more vertebrae than a giraffe's or a camel's.
facts.quote: It has also been noted for its flexibility in catching quick insects, as the number of vertebrae in its neck exceeds that of giraffes and camels.

facts.text: The brown thrasher inspired the name of Atlanta's former NHL team, the Atlanta Thrashers.
facts.quote: The brown thrasher also was the inspiration for the name of Atlanta's former National Hockey League team, the Atlanta Thrashers.

facts.text: Lesser yellowling chicks leave the nest just a few hours after hatching and can feed themselves right away.
facts.quote: Both parents brood and care for the precocial young, which leave the nest a few hours after hatching. They can feed themselves upon departure from the nest.

facts.text: Nesting lesser yellowlegs may swoop down to attack a predator or use distraction strategies to lure it away.
facts.quote: They may swoop down to attack the predator or use distraction strategies to lure it away.

facts.text: The name Tringa goes back to a thrush-sized, white-rumped, tail-bobbing wading bird mentioned by Aristotle.
facts.quote: The name Tringa is the Neo-Latin word given to the green sandpiper by the Italian naturalist Ulisse Aldrovandi in 1603 based on Ancient Greek trungas, a thrush-sized, white-rumped, tail-bobbing wading bird mentioned by Aristotle.

facts.text: When feeding, lesser yellowlegs move quickly with a high-stepping gait and neck outstretched, jabbing at prey with the bill.
facts.quote: They are very active when foraging, moving quickly with a high-stepping gait, neck outstretched, to pick at prey with quick jabs of the bill.

facts.text: Lesser yellowlegs sometimes forage at night.
facts.quote: Sometimes forages at night

facts.text: Greater yellowlegs chicks leave the nest within 24 hours of hatching.
facts.quote: The young leave the nest within 24 hours of hatching and then leave the vicinity of the nest within two days.

facts.text: When hunting in shallow water, these birds sometimes use their bills to stir up the water.
facts.quote: These birds forage in shallow water, sometimes using their bills to stir up the water.

facts.text: The greater yellowlegs eats insects and small fish, plus crustaceans, marine worms, frogs, seeds and berries.
facts.quote: They mainly eat insects and small fish, as well as crustaceans, marine worms, frogs, seeds and berries.

facts.text: Solitary sandpipers lay their eggs in old tree nests that songbirds such as thrushes have abandoned.
facts.quote: The sandpiper lays a clutch of 3–5 eggs in abandoned tree nests of songbird species, such as those of thrushes.

facts.text: Solitary sandpiper chicks are encouraged to drop to the ground soon after they hatch.
facts.quote: The young birds are encouraged to drop to the ground soon after hatching.

facts.text: Unlike most other scolopacids, both the solitary sandpiper and the green sandpiper nest in trees.
facts.quote: In addition, both species nest in trees, unlike most other scolopacids.

facts.text: Solitary sandpipers can pull snails out of their shells to eat them.
facts.quote: Food is small invertebrates: insects (such as mosquito larvae, young midges, grasshoppers, caterpillars and beetles), small crustaceans and molluscs (such as snails extracted from their shells), sometimes small frogs (primarily as tadpoles), picked off the mud as the bird works steadily around the edges of its chosen pond.

facts.text: This sandpiper often turns up at ditches too restricted for other waders, which tend to like a clear all-round view.
facts.quote: The solitary sandpiper is very much a bird of fresh water, and is often found in sites, such as ditches, too restricted for other waders, which tend to like a clear all-round view.

facts.text: The name Troglodytes means "hole dweller," a nod to how these wrens disappear into crevices to hunt insects or find shelter.
facts.quote: The name troglodytes means "hole dweller", and is a reference to the bird's tendency to disappear into crevices when hunting insects or to seek shelter.

facts.text: A male house wren gathers the sticks for the nest, and if the female doesn't approve, she throws the unwanted sticks to the ground.
facts.quote: The male wren finds dry sticks, which he adds to the nest. Once he is done, the female inspects the nest; but if she does not approve of the construction, she will throw any unwanted sticks to the ground.

facts.text: House wrens are known to occasionally puncture the eggshells of other birds' eggs nesting in their territory.
facts.quote: They are known to occasionally destroy the eggs of other birds nesting in their territory by puncturing the eggshell.

facts.text: House wrens are also known to stuff other birds' nests in their territory with sticks, making the nests unusable.
facts.quote: They are also known to fill up other birds' nests within its territory with sticks to make them unusable.

facts.text: On Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, King Friday XIII had a pet named Trog, a wooden wren on a stick who had his own song.
facts.quote: Troglodytes Aedon was one of the two pets of King Friday the XIII in Mister Rogers' Neighborhood. Trog, as the King called him, was a wooden wren on a stick, and Trog had his own song.

facts.text: The male builds a small number of nests, and they stay unlined until the female chooses one to use.
facts.quote: The male builds a small number of nests. These are called "cock nests" but are never lined until the female chooses one to use.

facts.text: In hard weather, winter wrens may roost in groups, family or strangers, gathered together for warmth.
facts.quote: In hard weather it may do so in parties, either consisting of the family or of many individuals gathered together for warmth.

facts.text: Winter wrens sometimes spend the night in old nests as well as snug holes.
facts.quote: At night, usually in winter, it often roosts, true to its scientific name, in dark retreats, snug holes and even old nests.

facts.text: Though it eats insects, the winter wren can stay in snowy places by foraging on bark and fallen logs.
facts.quote: Although it is an insectivore, it can remain in moderately cold and even snowy climates by foraging for insects on substrates such as bark and fallen logs.

facts.text: Winter wrens often build nests in bushes or in litter that floods leave piled up in tree branches.
