facts.quote: The normal round nest of grass, moss, lichens or leaves is tucked into a hole in a wall, tree trunk, crack in a rock or corner of a building, but it is often built in bushes, overhanging boughs or the litter which accumulates in branches washed by floods.

facts.text: Robins flock to fermented Pyracantha berries and, after eating enough, act intoxicated, even falling over while walking.
facts.quote: They will flock to fermented Pyracantha berries, and after eating sufficient quantities will exhibit intoxicated behavior, such as falling over while walking.

facts.text: Experiments have shown that robins can find earthworms underground just by using their listening skills.
facts.quote: Experiments have shown that it can find earthworms underground by simply using its listening skills.

facts.text: Robin chicks raise their tails to pass waste as a solid white clump, and a parent collects it before flying off.
facts.quote: Chicks are fed, and then raise tails for elimination of waste, a solid white clump that is collected by a parent prior to flying off.

facts.text: A robin family got minor publicity in the mid-1930s for their prominent nest on the Canadian side of the Peace Bridge.
facts.quote: The Peace Bridge robins were a family of American robins that attracted minor publicity in the mid-1930s for their prominent nest on the Canadian side of the Peace Bridge connecting Buffalo, New York, to Fort Erie, Ontario.

facts.text: Robins tagged in Alaska are known to travel as much as 3.5 times farther across seasons than robins tagged in Massachusetts.
facts.quote: The distance by which they migrate varies significantly depending on their initial habitat; a study found that individual robins tagged in Alaska are known to travel as much as 3.5 times farther across seasons than robins tagged in Massachusetts.

facts.text: The eastern kingbird's high-pitched, buzzing chirp is frequently compared to the sound of an electric fence.
facts.quote: The call is a high-pitched, buzzing and unmusical chirp, frequently compared to an electric fence.

facts.text: Eastern kingbirds aggressively defend their territory, even against much larger birds.
facts.quote: These birds aggressively defend their territory, even against much larger birds.

facts.text: Kingbird mobbing has been shown to keep ravens and crows from finding experimental nests placed near kingbird nests.
facts.quote: The aggressive mobbing behavior of eastern kingbirds has been shown to keep ravens and crows from finding experimental nests placed near kingbird nests.

facts.text: Eastern kingbirds in southern British Columbia may nest in open fields, in shrubs over open water, or even atop small stumps.
facts.quote: Eastern kingbirds in southern British Columbia may nest in open fields, in shrubs over open water, high up in trees, and even in the tops of small stumps.

facts.text: There are three European records of eastern kingbirds, all from the British Isles: two in Ireland and one in Scotland.
facts.quote: There are three European records, all from the British Isles: two from Ireland in October 2012 and September 2013, and one from Scotland in September 2016.

facts.text: A yellow-throated vireo turned up in Cornwall, Great Britain, in September 1990, a very rare visit for a bird from America.
facts.quote: They are very rare vagrants to western Europe; a September 1990 sighting from Kenidjack Valley in Cornwall, Great Britain, and September 1998 from Heligoland, a small German archipelago in the German Bight have been reported.

facts.text: Yellow-throated vireos hunt for insects high up in the trees.
facts.quote: They forage for insects high in trees.

facts.text: Before migration and in winter, these vireos eat berries, and are sometimes seen feeding on gumbo-limbo fruit.

facts.text: Mourning dove parents feed their young crop milk, even though the adults eat almost exclusively seeds.

facts.text: A male mourning dove stands on his mate's back to hand her nest material, and she builds it into the nest.

facts.text: Mourning doves sleep with the head resting between the shoulders, not tucked under the feathers like in many other species.

facts.text: White-throated sparrows scratch for food on the ground by kicking backward with both feet at the same time.

facts.text: A newer version of the song turns the "Peabody" triplets into "Cherry" doublets; it began in British Columbia and spread east.
facts.quote: This bird song begins in the same way as the typical song, but with a subtle difference: the repeating triplets, as in "Peabody", become doublets, as in "Cherry", ending with a final single tone. This new tune began to appear in British Columbia, Canada, and then spread east.

facts.text: One of its songs is often remembered as "Po-or Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody" or "O-oh sweet Canada, Canada, Canada."
facts.quote: This second song is commonly described by use of mnemonics with the cadence of "Po-or Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody" (or "O-oh sweet Canada, Canada, Canada").

facts.text: To a human ear, the white-throated sparrow's song often sounds out of tune.

facts.text: White-throated sparrows almost always pair up with a mate of the opposite color morph when breeding.

facts.text: White-crowned sparrows can stay half-awake for up to two weeks during migration thanks to a special kind of sleep.
facts.quote: The white-crowned sparrow is known for its unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, which allows it to stay half-awake for up to two weeks during migration.

facts.text: The white-crowned sparrow's half-awake sleep has been studied for possible uses to keep people alert in shift work and truck driving.
facts.quote: This effect has been studied for possible human alertness applications in shift work and truck driving.

facts.text: A white-crowned sparrow that showed up in Norfolk, England, in 2008 was honored with its picture in a church window.
facts.quote: In 2008 a white-crowned sparrow was spotted in Cley next the Sea in Norfolk, England. To commemorate the event an image of the bird was included in a window at St Margaret's Church.
